items.title: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (coronary artery disease, hypertension and peripheral vascular disease components)
items.body:
## 1.1 Myocardial oxygen supply and demand

Perioperative ischaemia is an imbalance between supply and demand. Myocardial O2 extraction is already high at rest (about 70 to 80%), so increased demand is met predominantly by increased coronary flow; extraction reserve is limited, rather than absent.

| Supply (determinants of flow) | Demand (determinants of consumption) |
|---|---|
| Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic DBP minus LVEDP (left ventricle) | Heart rate (the biggest lever; also shortens diastole) |
| Diastolic time (LV flow is mainly in diastole; falls with tachycardia) | Wall stress: preload/volume, afterload, radius and thickness (thin-wall spherical approximation σ = P × r / 2h; geometry and regional stress vary). This formula is stress, not wall tension. |
| Arterial O2 content (Hb, SaO2) | Contractility |
| Coronary patency, vascular tone and autoregulatory reserve; limits vary with stenosis, pressure, LVH and disease, so there is no universal 60–140 mmHg range. | Basal metabolic and shivering/thermal load |

> **Examiner favourite:** a tachycardic, hypotensive, anaemic patient with LVH is the worst case: demand up, DBP down, LVEDP up, O2 content down. Every part of anaesthetic management for IHD is built on this table.

**Types of myocardial injury (Fifth Universal Definition 2026; legacy type 1/type 2 terms retained for interpreting older studies):**

| Category | Mechanism | Perioperative example |
|---|---|---|
| Primary MI (broader than legacy type 1) | Acute coronary pathology: atherothrombosis, SCAD, vasospasm or embolism. New primary-MI classification is broader than old type 1. | Surgical stress, hypercoagulable state, catecholamine surge |
| Secondary MI (replaces legacy type 2) | Supply-demand mismatch without acute plaque event (most perioperative MIs) | Hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia |
| MINS (myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery) | Acute postoperative troponin elevation attributed to ischaemia within 30 days; symptoms/ECG changes are not required. Incidence varies by assay and population: 17.9% in the 2017 hsTnT VISION cohort, versus lower estimates using older assays. | Often detected by surveillance; higher mortality depends on troponin magnitude and clinical context. MINS is not synonymous with MI or a universal 10% mortality risk. |
| Non-ischaemic injury | Injury without evidence of ischaemia, e.g. myocarditis or critical-illness injury. Sepsis, PE and tachyarrhythmia may cause either non-ischaemic injury or secondary MI, depending on evidence. | Serial troponin plus clinical, ECG/imaging and haemodynamic assessment; chronic renal-associated elevation is not necessarily acute injury. |

**Perioperative MI in practice:**

- Many events occur early after surgery and are clinically silent because analgesia, sedation and competing postoperative symptoms mask ischaemia.
- ST depression and supply–demand imbalance are common, but ECG phenotype and mortality vary with population, assay and definition; the older figures of less than 2% ST elevation and 25% early mortality should not be applied universally.
- Troponin magnitude and persistent ischaemia identify higher risk.
- Decisions about antiplatelets, anticoagulation and invasive investigation need joint input from anaesthetist, intensivist, surgeon and cardiologist (Hughes et al., BJA Education 2024; Fifth UDMI 2026).

items.title: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + acute myocardial ischaemia crisis component at P2 HIGH
items.los: SS_CS 1.26; SS_IC 1.31; SS_CS 1.4 (myocardial ischaemia component); IT_RT 1.2 (acute myocardial ischaemia component)
items.body:
## 2.1 Recognition and diagnosis

**Clinical features:** central chest pain (often absent under GA or in diabetics, the elderly and after surgery), dyspnoea, sweating, nausea, arrhythmia, hypotension, new heart failure or cardiogenic shock. Perioperatively, suspect MI with unexplained hypotension, arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, new ST change, desaturation or agitation.

**Fifth Universal Definition of MI (2026):**

- Acute myocardial injury is a rise/fall in cardiac troponin with at least one value above the assay’s sex-specific 99th-percentile upper reference limit.
- MI requires acute injury plus clinical evidence of acute myocardial ischaemia, supported by symptoms, ECG, imaging or coronary findings as appropriate; imaging helps establish the aetiology.
- The updated categories are primary MI (acute coronary pathology, including atherothrombosis, SCAD, vasospasm or embolism), secondary MI (ischaemia from another acute condition causing supply–demand imbalance) and procedure-related MI after cardiac procedures.
- Legacy type 1/type 2 terminology remains in older trials.
- Non-cardiac postoperative MI is not automatically a cardiac procedure-related MI.
- Do not await troponin confirmation when acute coronary occlusion requires emergency reperfusion.
- For secondary MI, the 2026 document seeks objective confirmation: ischaemia associated with obstructive CAD without acute coronary pathology and/or new regional dysfunction or loss of viability attributable to the supply–demand event.
- Procedure-related MI applies to a cardiac-procedure complication within 30 days; later stent/graft pathology can be primary MI.

**ECG criteria (acute ischaemia):**

| Finding | Criteria |
|---|---|
| STEMI | New ST elevation at the J point in 2 contiguous leads: at least 1 mm in all leads except V2 to V3, where it is at least 2 mm in men aged 40 or over (2.5 mm under 40), at least 1.5 mm in women |
| NSTEMI / unstable angina | ST depression (at least 0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads), T wave inversion (at least 1 mm in leads with prominent R wave) or no change |
| Posterior MI | ST depression V1 to V3 with tall R waves; confirm with posterior leads V7 to V9 |
| Right ventricular MI | Inferior MI with right-sided ST elevation supports RV involvement. Avoid preload-reducing drugs in hypotension; give small reassessed fluid only if underfilled, not routine large-volume loading. |
| Equivalents | De Winter/hyperacute or posterior patterns may indicate occlusion. Apply validated Sgarbossa/modified criteria in LBBB/pacing; new LBBB alone is insufficient. Wellens suggests critical LAD disease requiring urgent assessment and avoidance of stress testing. Diffuse ST depression with aVR elevation suggests global subendocardial ischaemia, not specific left-main occlusion. |

| Territory | Leads | Artery |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior | V1 to V4 | LAD |
| Septal | V1 to V2 | LAD (septal perforators) |
| Lateral | I, aVL, V5 to V6 | LCx or diagonal |
| Inferior | II, III, aVF | Usually RCA, sometimes LCx; dominance and anatomy vary. |
| Posterior | ST depression V1 to V3 | RCA or LCx |
| RV | V4R | Proximal RCA |

**Troponin interpretation:**

- Hs-troponin can detect injury within the first few hours, but onset, peak and persistence vary by assay, reperfusion and infarct size; an early normal result does not exclude MI.
- Use a validated assay-specific 0/1 h or 0/2 h clinical decision pathway, with further sampling when needed.
- PE, sepsis, renal dysfunction, myocarditis, arrhythmia, takotsubo, dissection and contusion can cause injury; some also produce secondary ischaemic MI.
- A rise/fall alone does not prove atherothrombosis.
- CK-MB is largely obsolete when cardiac troponin is available.

## 2.2 Detection and investigation after surgery

- 12-lead ECG immediately and serially (compare with the preoperative ECG; absent baseline is a common exam trap).
- Serial hs-troponin; CK-MB only if troponin unavailable.
- Bedside echo (FoCUS/TTE): new RWMA, LV function, pericardial effusion, RV strain, valve lesion, mechanical complication.
- Chest X-ray, ABG, electrolytes (K, Mg), Hb, lactate, renal function, glucose, coagulation.
- Differential: PE, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, pericarditis, oesophageal pathology, takotsubo, myocarditis, anaemia or hypovolaemia with demand ischaemia.
- Coronary angiography for STEMI, high-risk NSTEMI, or unexplained shock.

## 2.3 Initial medical management

Standard ACS approach (National Heart Foundation of Australia / CSANZ Australian ACS guideline 2025, which replaced the 2016 version; ESC 2023; ACC/AHA 2025), adapted to the perioperative bleeding risk. Never delay reperfusion for investigations.

| Intervention | Details | Perioperative caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Give for SpO2 <90% or significant hypoxaemia; titrate and avoid hyperoxia. Australian 2025 ACS guidance advises not exceeding 96% when oxygen is used. DETO2X found no mortality benefit in initially normoxaemic patients, not definitive harm. |  |
| Aspirin | Australian 2025: 300 mg oral chewed/dissolved load, then 100 mg/day unless contraindicated; alternative guideline loading ranges differ. | Discuss with surgeon if fresh surgical bleeding |
| P2Y12 inhibitor | PCI-treated ACS commonly uses ticagrelor 180 mg or prasugrel 60 mg load; clopidogrel 300–600 mg in selected contexts. Prasugrel is contraindicated with previous stroke/TIA. Avoid routine NSTE-ACS pretreatment before anatomy is known when early angiography is planned; timing depends on pathway, bleeding and delay. | Bleeding risk; cardiology decision |
| Anticoagulation | UFH/enoxaparin/bivalirudin according to PCI, fibrinolysis or NSTE pathway. UFH 70–100 IU/kg is a common PCI bolus when no GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor is used; not a universal initial ACS dose. Adjust for renal function, age and prior anticoagulation. | Fresh surgical site: individualised |
| Analgesia | Titrated IV opioid (fentanyl or morphine); morphine delays absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors |  |
| Nitrates | GTN SL or IV for ongoing ischaemia, hypertension or pulmonary oedema | Avoid in hypotension, preload-dependent RV infarction or recent PDE-5 therapy (typically sildenafil/vardenafil <24 h, tadalafil <48 h; longer with impaired clearance). |
| Beta-blocker | IV only if tachycardic and hypertensive without heart failure or shock; early oral beta-blocker in stable patients | Avoid in shock, bradycardia, high-grade block, acute HF (COMMIT-CCS2: more cardiogenic shock with early IV metoprolol) |
| Statin | High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg |  |
| ACEi / ARB | Early in anterior MI, HF or LV dysfunction once stable | Avoid in shock or AKI |
| Antiemetic, anxiolytic | As needed |  |

- **2025 guideline updates.** Australian 2025 guideline (MJA 2026): acute coronary occlusion MI (ACOMI) ECG patterns are recognised beyond ST elevation;
- Hs-troponin is used in decision pathways;
- Stronger emphasis on timely primary PCI;
- Updated P2Y12 inhibitor timing in STEMI and NSTE-ACS;
- A stricter LDL-C target with PCSK9 inhibitors, beta-blockers and ARNI addressed in secondary prevention.
- ACC/AHA 2025: ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel in PCI-treated ACS;
- Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor for at least 12 months by default, with 1 to 3 months of DAPT then P2Y12 monotherapy reasonable in selected patients (Class 2a) and ticagrelor monotherapy from 1 month in patients who tolerated ticagrelor-based DAPT;
- With an oral anticoagulant, stop aspirin after 1 to 4 weeks and continue clopidogrel plus the anticoagulant;
- No routine non-culprit PCI in STEMI or NSTE-ACS with cardiogenic shock (Class 3: Harm);
- A microaxial flow pump may be reasonable in selected shock patients despite more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal failure;
- A Hb target of 100 g/L may be reasonable in ACS with anaemia.

**Anaesthetic and perioperative modifications:** treat the cause (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia), deepen anaesthesia or analgesia, maintain MAP (phenylephrine, noradrenaline), reduce HR, and escalate monitoring with invasive BP and TOE.

## 2.4 Reperfusion strategies

| Option | Indications and key points |
|---|---|
| Primary PCI | Emergency PCI for STEMI/acute coronary occlusion, ideally within local network targets. Australian 2025 strategy threshold: PCI deliverable within 120 min of first medical contact. ESC uses diagnosis-to-wire within 120 min; do not mix the clocks. Reperfuse within 12 h of symptoms and later with ongoing ischaemia, shock or life-threatening arrhythmia. |
| Fibrinolysis | When timely PCI is unavailable and symptoms <12 h, consider fibrinolysis only after contraindication assessment, then immediate transfer to a PCI centre. ESC target is lytic bolus within 10 min of STEMI diagnosis; other systems use FMC/door-to-needle targets. Rescue PCI immediately for failure/instability; successful lysis generally followed by angiography at 2–24 h. **Major recent surgery, active bleeding, intracranial pathology/stroke and suspected dissection may prohibit lysis; ESC lists major surgery/trauma/head injury within 1 month as an absolute contraindication**, so do not label recent**major surgery universally “relative”. Apply the current drug/network checklist.** PCI is usually preferred perioperatively. |
| Urgent angiography | Immediate invasive assessment for very-high-risk NSTE-ACS (shock, refractory/recurrent ischaemia, life-threatening arrhythmia or acute HF from ongoing ischaemia). Consider early <24 h for high-risk patients including GRACE >140; other inpatient timing is individualised, not automatically “all others <72 h”. |
| CABG | Emergency/urgent CABG for suitable anatomy when PCI is unsuccessful or unsuitable with ongoing jeopardy, or when surgery is required for a mechanical complication. Left-main/multivessel disease and diabetes inform Heart Team selection but do not by themselves mandate emergency CABG. |

![ACS reperfusion pathway · 1 decision, shock escalation](set11-fig1.png)

- Acute coronary occlusion patterns (including STEMI equivalents) require immediate reperfusion assessment without waiting for troponin.
- Very-high-risk NSTE-ACS also requires immediate angiography.
- In the diagram, use the corrected timings in table 2.4: Australian 2025 guidance prefers PCI within 120 min of first medical contact; 90 min is a system performance target, not the universal eligibility boundary.
- The arrows show alternative decisions, not a requirement to pass through shock or wait for deterioration.
- A GRACE score ≤140 does not automatically require angiography within 72 h.

## 2.5 Cardiogenic shock (SS_IC 1.31, SS_CS 1.26)

- Cardiogenic shock is cardiac dysfunction causing inadequate systemic perfusion: hypotension or a need for circulatory support with hypoperfusion (cold peripheries, oliguria, altered mentation, rising lactate).
- A classical invasive profile is cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m² with elevated filling pressure, but normotensive shock, early shock, RV-predominant and mixed shock occur; neither 30 min of hypotension, lactate >2 nor a high PCWP is mandatory in every presentation.
- Diagnose and treat evolving hypoperfusion early.

**Causes after MI:** pump failure (large infarct or impaired pre-existing reserve; no fixed percentage of LV loss is required), RV infarction, mechanical complications (acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture and tamponade), arrhythmia.

**SCAI staging:**

| Stage | Features |
|---|---|
| A At risk | Risk factors for shock; normal perfusion |
| B Beginning | Hypotension or tachycardia, no hypoperfusion |
| C Classic | Hypoperfusion requiring intervention (drugs, mechanical support); lactate often above 2 |
| D Deteriorating | Worsening despite initial support; escalation needed |
| E Extremis | Actual or impending circulatory collapse, refractory shock, often severe acidosis and arrest/CPR; multiple devices are not required to qualify. |

**Management principles:**

- **Emergency revascularisation of the culprit lesion is the key treatment (SHOCK trial:** survival benefit at 6 and 12 months). Culprit-only PCI is preferred (CULPRIT-SHOCK).
- **Haemodynamics:** noradrenaline is usually the first vasopressor for significant hypotension; SOAP II found fewer arrhythmias than dopamine and a mortality signal in its cardiogenic-shock subgroup, not a definitive standalone survival comparison in cardiogenic shock.
  - Add inotropy only for persistent low output after preload and perfusion-pressure assessment: dobutamine often starts at 2.5–5 micrograms/kg/min and is titrated; milrinone is an alternative, especially with beta-blockade, but can cause hypotension and accumulates in renal impairment.
  - No inotrope has a general proven survival advantage.
  - Adrenaline can worsen tachyarrhythmia, lactate and refractory shock; reserve for selected rescue circumstances.
  - Vasopressin may be an adjunct for a vasodilatory component.
- Avoid excess fluid, including in RV infarction. If underfilling is likely, consider a small fluid challenge (e.g. 250 mL) with immediate reassessment of stroke volume, congestion and perfusion; a dilated congested RV often deteriorates with additional volume.
- **Respiratory support:** oxygen, high-flow, NIV or intubation. Anaesthetic induction in shock is dangerous (see below).
- **Mechanical circulatory support (MCS):** see 2.6.
- **Treat arrhythmia, acidosis, anaemia (MINT: liberal transfusion considered), electrolytes.** Prevent hypothermia; after cardiac arrest follow current temperature-control and fever-prevention guidance rather than automatically inducing hypothermia.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line, central venous access, serial lactate, ScvO2, echo, consider PA catheter to guide complex shock (PCWP, CO, PVR; the right ventricle matters).

**Haemodynamic profile (Forrester / Stevenson):**

| Profile | Perfusion | Congestion | Typical therapy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm and dry | Adequate | No | Continue oral therapy |
| Warm and wet | Adequate | Yes | Diuretics, vasodilators |
| Cold and wet | Poor | Yes | Inotrope, vasopressor, MCS, diuretics |
| Cold and dry | Poor | No | Assess underfilling and fluid responsiveness; small reassessed bolus only if indicated. Consider inotrope for persistent low output; exclude RV congestion and obstruction. |

## 2.6 Mechanical circulatory support

| Device | Mechanism | Evidence | Key limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) | Counterpulsation in the descending aorta: inflates in diastole (raising diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion), deflates just before systole (reduces afterload, LV wall stress and O2 demand). Small rise in CO (about 0.5 L/min) | IABP-SHOCK II: no survival benefit from routine IABP in revascularised MI shock without mechanical complications. Selected mechanical complications/bridging remain separate indications. | Aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, severe peripheral vascular disease; works only with a rhythm that triggers and adequate native output; limb ischaemia, bleeding, thrombocytopenia |
| Impella (percutaneous LV assist, axial flow) | Pumps blood from LV to ascending aorta, giving up to 2.5 to 5.5 L/min depending on model | DanGer Shock (STEMI shock): lower 180-day mortality, more bleeding and limb ischaemia | Haemolysis, vascular complications, LV thrombus is a contraindication, mechanical aortic valve |
| VA-ECMO | Venous drainage through pump/oxygenator to arterial circulation; flow depends on cannula and patient. Supports systemic flow and oxygenation but raises LV afterload. Assess LV distension/aortic opening and use unloading when indicated, not automatically in every case. | ECLS-SHOCK, ECMO-CS: no mortality benefit in unselected shock | Bleeding, limb ischaemia, stroke, harlequin (differential hypoxia) syndrome, infection |
| TandemHeart and dedicated RV support | Standard TandemHeart drains LA via transseptal cannula to an arterial return: LV unloading/support. Dedicated RVAD configurations (e.g. RA-to-PA pump/ProtekDuo) are different; VA-ECMO may support RV failure with systemic shock. | Small series | Large-bore access, anticoagulation, bleeding/vascular injury; device choice depends on LV/RV failure and oxygenation. Standard TandemHeart is not intrinsically an RVAD. |

**IABP waveform. In the 1:**

- 2 assist mode the arterial trace alternates between an assisted and an unassisted beat.
- Features of a correct assisted beat: the dicrotic notch replaced by a sharp V-shaped inflation point;
- **diastolic augmentation** (often above native systolic pressure, but this is not required in every patient);
- **assisted end-diastolic pressure** lower than unassisted end-diastolic;
- **assisted systolic pressure** lower than the unassisted systolic.
- Timing errors: early inflation (before the notch: aortic valve closes prematurely, reducing SV), late inflation (reduced augmentation), early deflation (loss of diastolic augmentation and reduced effective unloading), late deflation (balloon remains inflated into systole, increasing afterload).

![IABP 1:2 arterial pressure trace · points A to F](set11-fig2.png)

Compare the assisted and unassisted values: E should sit below A and F below B if counterpulsation is working.

**Physiological principle:** raising diastolic aortic pressure improves coronary perfusion (the effect depends on stenosis severity, collateral flow and distal resistance; flow is not simply fixed in every stenosed vessel), and systolic unloading reduces LV wall tension, so oxygen supply rises while demand falls.

> **Pitfall:** an IABP relies on native cardiac ejection and provides modest augmentation rather than full forward flow. It is inadequate as sole support for profound pump failure or cardiac arrest, but selected refractory shock or mechanical complications may still justify its use as a bridge after specialist assessment; IABP-SHOCK II does not exclude every such indication.

## 2.7 Anaesthesia for acute revascularisation (SS_CS 1.26)

**For primary PCI or emergency angiography:**

### Preop

- Most patients can be managed with local anaesthetic and light sedation; the case for GA is airway protection in unstable patients with shock, cardiac arrest, respiratory failure or agitation.
- Avoid sedation that causes hypotension or hypoventilation.

### Intraop

- Consider the contrast load (renal), radiation and positioning.
- Reperfusion arrhythmias (accelerated idioventricular rhythm, VF), bleeding and vascular access complications are the major concerns.

### Postop

After PCI, monitor access-site/retroperitoneal bleeding, rhythm, ongoing ischaemia, renal function and antiplatelet continuity; use CCU/ICU according to shock and respiratory status.

**For emergency CABG (see Set 13 for CPB):**

### Preop

- Preoperative: DAPT bleeding risk and platelet availability; stabilise with tailored vasoactive support and selected MCS when indicated; IABP is not routine for uncomplicated MI-related shock.

### Intraop

- Induction in shock: invasive arterial line before induction; titrate induction agent (etomidate or ketamine; reduced dose), maintain MAP with noradrenaline or vasopressin, avoid tachycardia and hypotension; fentanyl-based balanced anaesthesia.
  - Anticipate low cardiac output at induction because sympatholysis unmasks reduced reserve.
- Hypotension at induction in a failing ventricle is treated with vasopressor and inotrope early, not fluid alone.

### Postop

After emergency CABG, ICU care addresses bleeding, tamponade, low output, ischaemia, ventilation, rhythm and organ perfusion; resume secondary prevention and antithrombotic therapy according to surgical haemostasis and graft/ACS indications.

**For anaesthesia in patients with recent PCI or MI undergoing urgent non-cardiac surgery:** follow Topic 1 (antiplatelet continuation, high-risk perioperative environment, post-operative HDU, troponin surveillance).

## 2.8 Mechanical complications and RV infarction

| Complication | Timing | Features | Management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Papillary muscle rupture (acute severe MR) | 2 to 7 days (posteromedial papillary muscle, single blood supply: PDA) | Pulmonary oedema, shock, soft murmur because of equalised pressures, large v wave | Urgent surgical/Heart Team assessment; afterload reduction if BP permits, tailored support and selected IABP/MCS as bridge. |
| Ventricular septal rupture | 3 to 5 days | New loud pansystolic murmur, left-to-right shunt, RV overload | IABP, surgical or percutaneous closure |
| Free wall rupture | Can occur early or later; classical subacute windows are not exclusion criteria. | Tamponade, PEA | Immediate surgical resuscitation/repair. Controlled pericardial drainage may be a bridge for critical tamponade when surgery is not immediately available; uncontrolled decompression can worsen bleeding. |
| RV infarction | With inferior MI | Hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs | Preserve AV synchrony/perfusion; fluid only for demonstrated underfilling with immediate reassessment. Avoid nitrates/diuresis when hypotensive/preload depleted; a congested RV may need decongestion and inotropic support. |
| Arrhythmia | Reperfusion; VT/VF within 48 h |  | Defibrillation, amiodarone, correct K/Mg, beta-blocker |

## 2.9 After the acute event

- After ACS: DAPT for 12 months by default, modified for bleeding risk and any oral anticoagulation; high-intensity lipid lowering, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation and risk-factor treatment.
- ACEi/ARB and beta-blockers have clear indications with LV dysfunction/HF or other relevant conditions; lifelong beta-blockade is not automatic after every uncomplicated MI with preserved EF.
- MRA is indicated in selected post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40% and HF or diabetes if potassium and renal function permit.
- Primary-prevention ICD assessment generally waits at least 40 days after MI and reassesses after ≥3 months of optimised therapy/revascularisation; EF alone is insufficient and secondary-prevention indications differ.

items.title: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (left heart failure component); SS_CS 1.4 (filling status; LV systolic and diastolic function); SS_IC 1.35 (heart failure in intensive care)
items.body:
## 3.1 Definitions and classification

**Heart failure (HF):** clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs caused by structural or functional cardiac abnormality, with raised natriuretic peptides or objective evidence of congestion.

| Type | LVEF | Features |
|---|---|---|
| HFrEF | <50% in ESC 2026; ≤40% in legacy trials and AHA/ACC 2022. | Reduced-EF HF requires clinical syndrome plus objective evidence; not every LV is dilated. |
| Legacy HFmrEF | 41 to 49% | Retired as a separate category in ESC 2026, now within HFrEF. Retain 41–49% when discussing older studies/other guidelines. |
| HFpEF | 50% or more | Diastolic dysfunction, LVH, raised filling pressures, LA enlargement; often elderly, hypertensive, diabetic, obese, women |
| HFimpEF | Baseline 40% or less, improved by 10 points to above 40% | Continue therapy |

**Staging:** ACC/AHA stages A to D (A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C symptomatic, D refractory). NYHA class I to IV by symptoms: I no limitation; II slight, symptoms on ordinary activity; III marked, symptoms on less than ordinary activity; IV symptoms at rest.

**Acute HF presentations:** acute decompensated chronic HF (most), acute pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, hypertensive HF, isolated right HF.

## 3.2 Pathophysiology

- **Systolic dysfunction:** reduced contractility and ejection.
  - Low stroke volume activates the sympathetic nervous system (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), RAAS (sodium and water retention, afterload), and natriuretic peptide release.
  - Chronic activation causes remodelling: eccentric hypertrophy, dilatation, functional MR, and arrhythmia.
- **Diastolic dysfunction:** impaired relaxation (active, energy-dependent early diastole) and increased stiffness (passive compliance).
  - The LV pressure-volume curve shifts up and left: small volume changes cause large pressure changes.
  - Dependence on atrial contraction often increases, but its contribution varies with rate, age and disease; AF and tachycardia may therefore be badly tolerated.

| Feature | Systolic dysfunction | Diastolic dysfunction |
|---|---|---|
| End-systolic pressure-volume relationship | Shifted down and right (reduced Ees) | May have preserved or increased chamber systolic stiffness; not uniformly normal. |
| End-diastolic pressure-volume relationship | Shifted right (dilated) | Shifted up and left (stiff) |
| EDV | Increased | Normal or reduced |
| EF | Reduced | Preserved |
| Preload response | Plateaus on a flat Starling curve | Pressure–volume relation is steep: a small volume rise can markedly raise filling pressure. This does not demonstrate fluid responsiveness. |
| Poorly tolerated | Afterload rise, negative inotropes | Tachycardia, AF, hypovolaemia and hypervolaemia, ischaemia |

## 3.4 Chronic management of HF (basis of perioperative continuation)

| Drug class | Role | Perioperative note |
|---|---|---|
| ACEi / ARB / ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) | Mortality benefit in HFrEF (SOLVD, PARADIGM-HF) | Individualise continuation/withholding by HF indication, BP, renal status and local guidance. The ≥36 h washout applies when switching between ACEi and ARNI in either direction, not a routine 36 h perioperative ARNI omission. No ACEi/ARNI overlap. |
| Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) | Mortality benefit (CIBIS-II, MERIT-HF, COPERNICUS) | Continue; avoid abrupt withdrawal |
| MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) | MRA benefit in HFrEF and, per ESC 2026, across the EF spectrum; select agent and monitor potassium/renal function. Composite benefit is not proof of mortality reduction in each phenotype. | Check K and renal function |
| SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) | DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced; EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER in HFpEF | **Withhold 3 to 4 days before surgery** (euglycaemic ketoacidosis) |
| Loop diuretics | Symptom control | Adjust to congestion, fasting and volume status; do not universally omit in congested HF. Resume/continue with electrolyte and renal monitoring. |
| Ivabradine | SHIFT: HR above 70 despite beta-blocker | Continue |
| Digoxin | Symptoms and rate control | Check level, K |
| Hydralazine plus nitrate | Additional option for selected symptomatic HFrEF (including evidence in self-identified Black patients in A-HeFT) or intolerance of RAAS therapy; not an ancestry-only prescription. |  |
| Device therapy | ICD/CRT eligibility depends on EF, symptoms, aetiology, QRS morphology/duration, optimised therapy, timing and expected survival; EF ≤35% alone is insufficient. | Create a device-specific plan for EMI and pacing dependence; not every device requires reprogramming. |

**ESC 2026 update:**

- HFrEF now includes LVEF <50% and HFpEF ≥50%; HFmrEF is retired in this classification, although older thresholds remain essential when reading trials and other guidelines.
- Foundational HFrEF treatment comprises RAAS inhibition (preferably ARNI when appropriate), evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor.
- SGLT2 inhibitors and MRAs now have recommendations across the EF range; in HFpEF, benefit is largely fewer HF events and a composite benefit must not be described as proven mortality reduction for each drug.
- Treat congestion, BP, AF, ischaemia and comorbidities; consider obesity-directed therapy in selected HFpEF.
- Once stable, initiate and optimise therapy before discharge and early after discharge.
- Monitor BP, potassium, renal function and volume state; continue treatment after EF improvement.

## 3.6 Heart failure in the intensive care unit (SS_IC 1.35)

**Aim:** treat the cause, relieve congestion, restore perfusion, and protect organs.

**Initial assessment: perfusion and congestion profile (warm/cold, wet/dry; see Topic 2); ECG, troponin, BNP, lactate, echo, CXR. Identify precipitants using the mnemonic CHAMP:**

- Acute **C**oronary syndrome, **H**ypertensive emergency, **A**rrhythmia, acute **M**echanical cause (valve, VSD, rupture), **P**ulmonary embolism.
- Others: infection, non-adherence, anaemia, thyroid, drugs (NSAIDs, negative inotropes), fluid overload, renal failure.

**Treatment:**

| Goal | Therapy |
|---|---|
| Oxygenation and breathing | Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 90% or PaO2 below 60 mmHg (oxygen in non-hypoxaemic patients causes vasoconstriction and lowers cardiac output; ESC 2021); CPAP or NIV as soon as possible for respiratory distress (respiratory rate above 25, SpO2 below 90%), with CPAP about 10 cmH2O usually effective (see Topic 5); intubate for exhaustion, shock or failure of NIV |
| Decongestion | IV loop diuretic (ESC 2021): start with 1 to 2 times the usual daily oral dose as IV furosemide, or 20 to 40 mg if diuretic-naive; give as 2 to 3 boluses a day or an infusion (a single daily bolus is discouraged because of post-dose sodium retention). DOSE trial: high-dose (2.5 times) vs low-dose and bolus vs infusion gave similar symptom outcomes, with more transient creatinine rise at high dose. Add thiazide (metolazone) or acetazolamide (ADVOR) for resistance; ultrafiltration if refractory |
| Vasodilators | GTN or nitroprusside for hypertensive, congested patients with SBP above 110 (benefit mainly in APO) |
| Perfusion (low-output state) | Use inotropy only for low output with hypoperfusion after assessment. Dobutamine commonly 2.5–10 micrograms/kg/min initially, titrated (higher doses sometimes required). Milrinone about 0.125–0.75 micrograms/kg/min, renal adjustment and usually no bolus in hypotension. Beta-independent inodilators may suit selected beta-blocked patients, but are not universally preferred or proven to improve survival. Noradrenaline may start around 0.02–0.1 micrograms/kg/min and be titrated to perfusion; 0.2–1.0 is not a required starting range. Add vasopressin selectively for vasodilation; reassess LV/RV and the need for MCS. |
| Mechanical support | IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO as a bridge to recovery, device or transplant (see Topic 2.6). ECMO also treats refractory VF/cardiac arrest (ECPR) |
| Rhythm | Cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias; amiodarone; pacing for bradycardia |
| Renal and metabolic | Correct K and Mg; monitor creatinine (cardiorenal syndrome); renal replacement or ultrafiltration if needed |
| Other | Venous thromboprophylaxis, nutrition, early mobilisation, palliative care input in advanced HF |

**ESC 2026 decompensated HF guidance, with BJA Education pathophysiology and practical assessment:**

- **Diuretic response check:** assess early with a spot urine sodium at 2 h (satisfactory above 50 to 70 mmol/L) and/or urine output above 100 to 150 mL/h over the first 6 h.
  - If inadequate, double the IV loop dose; if still inadequate, add a thiazide, metolazone or acetazolamide with close electrolyte and renal monitoring.
  - Doses of 400–600 mg/day are sometimes required; this is not an absolute ceiling, and severe renal impairment may require higher specialist-directed doses with close monitoring.
  - Continue to full decongestion before discharge, because persistent congestion predicts readmission and death.
  - The algorithm is expert opinion.
- **Vasodilators:** may be considered for symptom relief when SBP is above 110 mmHg; two randomised trials of early intensive vasodilation did not beat high-dose diuretic, so no regimen is favoured.
  - Use extreme caution with LVH or severe aortic stenosis.
  - GTN boluses of 1–2 mg have been described for severe hypertensive pulmonary oedema in closely monitored specialist protocols; they are not routine initial doses and can cause profound hypotension.
  - A titrated infusion is appropriate in many patients.
- **Inotropes:** reserved for LV systolic dysfunction with low output and low SBP (for example below 90 mmHg) and poor organ perfusion; adrenergic inotropes cause tachycardia, ischaemia and arrhythmia and can increase mortality.
  - In the absence of hypotension or shock they are not recommended.
  - Selected advanced-HF bridging or palliative inotrope use is a specialist exception; treatment is not determined by SBP alone.
- **Vasopressors:** noradrenaline preferred over dopamine (SOAP II cardiogenic shock subgroup: more arrhythmia and higher mortality with dopamine) and over adrenaline (a trial in MI cardiogenic shock stopped early for more refractory shock with adrenaline; an observational meta-analysis reported an association with higher mortality, subject to confounding by indication).
- **Opiates:** routine use is not recommended (retrospective association with more ventilation, ICU admission and mortality; NICE advises against); consider for severe pain, anxiety or palliation.
- **Other:** venous thromboprophylaxis if not already anticoagulated and bleeding risk permits.
  - For AF, urgently cardiovert if instability is attributable to the rhythm; otherwise choose rate/rhythm therapy for haemodynamics and EF.
  - IV digoxin loading, if selected, must account for age, lean body weight, renal function, prior doses, interactions, potassium and levels; do not automatically give 0.5 mg to every patient with HR >110.
- **Mechanical support:** unselected use is not supported and needs a multidisciplinary shock team.
  - IABP is not routine in post-MI shock (IABP-SHOCK II) but may be considered for drug-refractory shock not due to ACS.
  - VA-ECMO raises LV afterload and congestion, so assess for LV distension, absent aortic opening and pulmonary oedema and add LV unloading when indicated (e.g. vent or Impella), balancing procedural risks; it may be used in fulminant myocarditis.
- **Pulmonary artery catheter:** not routine (NICE and AHA); use in complex or refractory ADHF.
  - Static CVP and PAWP do not predict fluid responsiveness, so measure the cardiac output response to a fluid bolus or passive leg raise.
  - An elevated PAWP supports raised left-sided filling pressure in context; >16 mmHg alone neither establishes HF nor defines its severity.
- **Other practical points:** titrate oxygen for hypoxaemia; positive pressure can unload the LV but reduce venous return and worsen RV loading.
  - Continue or temporarily adjust HF drugs according to perfusion, renal function, potassium and indication, rather than a single universal SBP/eGFR cut-off.
  - Continue chronic beta-blockade in stable patients, but reduce/withhold in shock, symptomatic bradycardia or advanced AV block as appropriate.
  - Dobutamine provides temporary haemodynamic support; a 3–5-day infusion has no established durable 30-day benefit, and observational timing comparisons do not prove a universal “start within 6 h” rule.

**Pulmonary artery catheter in HF:** ESCAPE showed no benefit of routine PAC-guided therapy in acute decompensated HF, so reserve it for shock of uncertain mechanism, refractory shock, transplant or LVAD assessment and pulmonary hypertension.

**Cardiogenic shock after non-ischaemic causes:** myocarditis, takotsubo, peripartum cardiomyopathy, decompensated chronic HF, drug toxicity. Same principles; VA-ECMO is a bridge to recovery (for example fulminant myocarditis).

**Advanced HF therapies:**

- LVAD (HeartMate 3, destination therapy or bridge to transplant), heart transplant.
- Anaesthetic considerations for the LVAD patient: reduced or absent pulsatility may occur (use arterial monitoring when indicated; Doppler opening pressure approximates MAP best when pulsatility is low and may resemble systolic pressure when pulsatility is present), preload and RV function dependence, anticoagulated, driveline infection, and pump thrombosis.
- Avoid hypovolaemia, high PVR, and tachyarrhythmia.

items.title: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (valvular heart disease component); SS_CS 1.4 (valve pathology component)
items.body:
## 4.1 General principles

- Severe stenotic lesions limit flow res**erv**e and can poorly tolerate tachycardia, hypovolaemia and abrupt vasodilation; the physiology differs between AS and MS and is not identical to absolute fixed output. Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (AS) and mitral stenosis (MS) carry the highest perioperative risk.
- Regurgitant lesions are volume-loaded and tolerate vasodilation, with avoidance of bradycardia and excessive afterload, better than stenotic lesions.
- Acute valve failure (acute MR, AR) is far worse than chronic disease because the ventricle has not adapted.
- Preoperative assessment aims to define severity, symptoms, ventricular function, pulmonary pressures, rhythm, and anticoagulation.
- Elective non-cardiac surgery should be deferred for severe symptomatic stenosis until the valve is treated (surgical or transcatheter) unless the surgery is urgent.
- Endocarditis prophylaxis: distinguish infection prevention for surgery from IE-specific prophylaxis.
  - Follow current Australian/NZ guidance for high-risk cardiac conditions and at-risk dental procedures; Australian/NZ recommendations include relevant rheumatic-heart-disease populations, so a US-only list is incomplete.
  - Core high-risk groups include prosthetic valves/material, previous IE and selected congenital lesions.
  - AHA does not recommend routine IE prophylaxis for non-dental GI/GU procedures without infection; ESC 2023 allows consideration for selected high-risk patients undergoing invasive non-dental procedures.
  - Treat active infection and use procedure-specific surgical prophylaxis.
  - Check the local dental/IE guideline for the precise lesion and procedure.

## 4.2 Overview of severity and haemodynamics

| Lesion | Severe criteria (echo) | Ventricular response | Core haemodynamic goals |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aortic stenosis | AV area below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6), mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more, dimensionless index below 0.25. Low-flow low-gradient forms exist | Concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction, high LVEDP, subendocardial ischaemia | Euvolaemia, avoid marked rate extremes, preserve sinus rhythm and systemic/coronary perfusion; no obligatory volume loading or fixed HR target. |
| Aortic regurgitation | Regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, fraction 50% or more, EROA 0.3 cm2 or more, vena contracta above 0.6 cm, pressure half-time below 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta | Eccentric dilatation (chronic); wide pulse pressure | Adequate preload without overload; avoid bradycardia and excessive SVR; maintain forward flow/contractility. High-normal rate is a guide, not a mandatory 80–100 target. |
| Mitral stenosis | MVA ≤1.5 cm² denotes clinically severe/significant rheumatic MS for intervention decisions; older echo grading calls <1.0 severe. Gradient is flow/rate dependent. PHT-derived MVA ≈220/PHT, but PHT is unreliable with altered compliance/AR or after intervention; 150 ms alone is not a universal severe-MS criterion. | LA dilatation, AF, pulmonary hypertension, RV failure; normal LV | Preload adequate not excessive, rate slow (60 to 80, long diastole), sinus rhythm, keep SVR, avoid rises in PVR |
| Mitral regurgitation | EROA 0.4 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, vena contracta 0.7 cm or more, systolic flow reversal in pulmonary veins | LV dilatation, normal or low-normal EF 'flatters' LV (EF below 60% already indicates dysfunction) | Euvolaemia; avoid bradycardia and excessive afterload, support LV/RV as needed. Do not use “full” to justify fluid overload. |
| Tricuspid | Rare in isolation | RV and RA overload | Maintain preload, avoid raised PVR |

![valve lesions by heart rate and afterload goal](set11-fig3.png)

- Use the diagram as a qualitative mnemonic: preserve adequate filling without congestion and maintain systemic perfusion without indiscriminately raising SVR.
- Individualise rate for lesion severity, ventricular function and ischaemia rather than prescribing a fixed range.
- Shorter diastole reduces AR; MR is systolic, so its rationale is avoiding bradycardia and excessive afterload while maintaining forward flow.
- MS primarily requires rate control and avoidance of pulmonary congestion; raising SVR does not relieve its obstruction.

## 4.3 Aortic stenosis (most examinable)

**Aetiology: age-related calcific degeneration (most common), bicuspid valve (younger patients), rheumatic. Historical untreated natural history (not current individual prognosis):**

- Long asymptomatic phase with slow progression (progression varies widely; older cohorts reported peak velocity rising about 0.3 m/s, mean gradient about 7 mmHg/year and area falling about 0.1 cm²/year);
- After the onset of symptoms, mean survival falls steeply: **angina about 5 years, syncope about 3 years, heart failure about 1 to 2 years**;
- High risk of sudden death once symptomatic.

**Echocardiographic features of haemodynamically significant AS:**

| Feature | Finding |
|---|---|
| Valve morphology | Thickened, calcified leaflets with restricted opening; bicuspid appearance in PLAX or SAX (TOE short axis at 30 to 60 degrees) |
| Peak velocity (CW Doppler through the valve) | 4.0 m/s or more (severe); 3.0 to 3.9 moderate |
| Mean gradient | 40 mmHg or more (severe) |
| Valve area (continuity equation) | AVA = (LVOT area x LVOT VTI) / AV VTI; below 1.0 cm2 severe |
| Dimensionless index (DVI) | LVOT VTI / AV VTI below 0.25 |
| LV | Concentric LVH, preserved or reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction (E/e' raised) |
| Other | Post-stenotic aortic root dilation, MR, LA enlargement, pulmonary hypertension (late) |
| Low-flow low-gradient AS | Low flow: SVI ≤35 mL/m² with AVA ≤1 cm² and mean gradient <40. Classical low-flow low-gradient: LVEF <50%; paradoxical: LVEF ≥50%. Check measurements/BP, use dobutamine stress in selected reduced-EF cases and CT valve calcium in discordant cases. ESC 2025 supportive calcium thresholds approximately >1200 AU women/>2000 men; US thresholds differ. Interpret probability, sex and context rather than one binary score. |

**Pathophysiology:**

- Fixed LV outflow obstruction leads to concentric hypertrophy, raised LVEDP, increased wall tension and O2 demand, and reduced coronary flow reserve from elevated LVEDP and low DBP (subendocardial ischaemia in the absence of coronary disease).
- Loss of atrial kick (AF, junctional rhythm) causes sudden decompensation.
- Stroke-volume reserve is limited in advanced AS; excessive tachycardia also impairs filling and perfusion, so output cannot safely be maintained simply by raising heart rate.

**Anaesthetic management of severe AS:**

## 4.4 Aortic regurgitation

**Aetiology:** valve disease (bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis) or root dilatation (Marfan, hypertension, ankylosing spondylitis, aortic dissection).

**Pathophysiology:** volume overload, eccentric hypertrophy, large stroke volume with wide pulse pressure (peripheral signs: collapsing pulse, de Musset, Quincke), low DBP and reduced coronary perfusion. Acute AR (endocarditis, dissection): LV cannot dilate, so LVEDP rises, premature MV closure, pulmonary oedema and shock.

## 4.5 Mitral stenosis

**Aetiology:** rheumatic heart disease (dominant in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori and Pacific communities in Australasia), calcific degeneration, congenital.

**Pathophysiology: obstruction between LA and LV raises LA pressure, then pulmonary venous and arterial pressure, causing pulmonary congestion, pulmonary hypertension and RV failure. The LV is underfilled with preserved EF. Heart rate dictates filling time:**

- Tachycardia shortens diastole, raising the gradient (gradient depends on flow and diastolic time squared) and LA pressure, causing APO.
- AF is common (loss of atrial kick, thromboembolism, stroke).

**MS severity definitions (Holmes, BJA Education 2017):**

- The older echo criteria are mild MVA 1.6 to 2.0 cm2, moderate 1.0 to 1.5 cm2 and severe below 1.0 cm2, with mean gradient above 5 mmHg moderate and above 10 mmHg severe, and pressure half-time 220 ms or more severe.
- The ESC/EACTS threshold of 1.5 cm2 or less marks clinically significant MS, the point at which intervention is considered.
- A normal valve area is 4 to 6 cm2 and symptoms usually appear below 2.0 cm2.
- Up to 40% of patients with severe MS develop AF.
- Asymptomatic patients with PASP <50 mmHg may tolerate surgery, but this does not guarantee safety: severity, functional capacity, rhythm, RV function and surgical stress still matter.
- Aim for good rate control without excessive bradycardia; <70/min is not mandatory in every setting.
- Avoid factors increasing PVR, including nitrous oxide when pulmonary hypertension is important.

**Perioperative management (including laparoscopic surgery):**

## 4.7 Prosthetic valves and anticoagulation

| Type | Antithrombotic therapy | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanical AVR (bileaflet, no risk factors) | Warfarin INR 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) | Lifelong |
| Mechanical AVR with risk factors (AF, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable) or older-generation valve | INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5) |  |
| Mechanical MVR | INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5) | Higher thrombotic risk than AVR |
| Bioprosthetic | Surgical aortic bioprosthesis: aspirin or VKA initially according to guideline/risk; mitral/tricuspid position commonly needs initial VKA. Duration (often 3 months, sometimes 3–6) and long-term OAC depend on position, AF and other indications. |  |
| TAVI | Single antiplatelet (usually low-dose aspirin) without another OAC indication; OAC alone when indicated unless recent PCI requires combination. Do not prescribe routine DAPT/DOAC solely because TAVI was performed. |  |
| DOAC | Contraindicated with mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN, dabigatran) |  |

## 4.8 Assessment of valve disease (SS_CS 1.4)

| Modality | Information |
|---|---|
| Clinical | Murmur (AS: ejection systolic radiating to carotids; MR: pansystolic to axilla; MS: mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap; AR: early diastolic decrescendo), pulse character, S3/S4, JVP, signs of RV failure |
| ECG | LVH, AF, left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), conduction disease |
| Echo | Valve morphology and mobility, severity (above), chamber size, EF, PASP, RV function, vegetations; TOE for detail and intraoperative use |
| CMR / CT | Quantification of regurgitation; CT for TAVI planning and calcium scoring |
| Catheterisation | Invasive haemodynamics when non-invasive findings are inconclusive; CAD assessment before intervention uses age/risk and CT or invasive angiography as appropriate, not routine catheterisation for every valve patient. |

**Intraoperative TOE views for valves:** ME 4-chamber, ME 2-chamber, ME LAX (MV), ME AV SAX (AV morphology), ME AV LAX (AR jet width, root), TG LAX and deep TG (CW Doppler gradient), colour Doppler jets. Use the Carpentier classification (Type I normal leaflet motion, II prolapse, III restricted: IIIa systolic and diastolic, IIIb systolic) for MR mechanism.

items.title: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.body:
## 5.1 Pathophysiology

**Starling forces across the pulmonary capillary:**

- Jv = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - sigma x (pi_c - pi_i)].
- Oedema forms when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, oncotic pressure falls, permeability rises (sigma falls, Kf rises), or lymphatic drainage is overwhelmed.
- Lymphatic reserve is substantial but variable; oedema develops when filtration exceeds effective clearance, and the alveolar epithelium is the final barrier, so oedema appears in the interstitium (Kerley lines, peribronchial cuffing) before flooding alveoli.
- The classical Starling equation is a teaching model; the endothelial glycocalyx and subglycocalyx oncotic gradient refine modern interpretation.

| Category | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiogenic / hydrostatic | Raised pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure; PAOP may be elevated but 18 mmHg is not an absolute diagnostic boundary. | LV failure (ischaemia, hypertensive crisis, cardiomyopathy), MS, acute MR or AR, arrhythmia, fluid overload, renal failure, TACO |
| Non-cardiogenic (permeability) | Increased permeability; hydrostatic and permeability mechanisms can coexist. A normal PAOP is not required for ARDS. | ARDS, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, TRALI, pancreatitis |
| Mixed or other | Reduced oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, negative pressure | Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (laryngospasm, airway obstruction), neurogenic, re-expansion, high-altitude, opioid or salicylate toxicity, upper-airway obstruction |

**Physiological consequences:** reduced compliance (increased work of breathing), shunt and V/Q mismatch (hypoxaemia), and increased sympathetic drive (hypertension, tachycardia, high afterload creates a vicious circle). Positive pressure acts by reducing venous return (preload), lowering LV transmural pressure (afterload), recruiting alveoli, and reducing work of breathing.

**Perioperative triggers:**

- Fluid overload or TACO, myocardial ischaemia, new arrhythmia (AF), hypertensive crisis (emergence), negative pressure pulmonary oedema (after extubation with laryngospasm or airway obstruction; can occur at any age, often reported in young, fit patients, resolves in 24 to 48 h), aspiration, anaphylaxis, TRALI or transfusion-associated circulatory overload, neurogenic oedema (subarachnoid haemorrhage, head injury), sepsis or SIRS, drug reaction (protamine), and pre-eclampsia; PE is an important acute-dyspnoea differential rather than a usual cause of alveolar oedema.

## 5.2 Clinical features and diagnosis

- **Symptoms:** acute breathlessness, orthopnoea, agitation, cough with pink frothy sputum.
- **Signs:** tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension (or shock), S3 gallop, bilateral crackles and wheeze ('cardiac asthma'), raised JVP, hypoxaemia.
- **Investigations:** ABG (hypoxaemia, with hypercapnia if fatigue develops), ECG, troponin and natriuretic peptides interpreted with renal function, rhythm and obesity.
  - CXR may show perihilar shadowing, cardiomegaly, Kerley lines or effusions, but distributions overlap and normal heart size does not exclude cardiogenic oedema.
  - Lung ultrasound showing multiple bilateral B-lines supports interstitial syndrome but is not specific for cardiogenic oedema; interpret pleura, distribution, consolidation and the clinical picture (Kim and Lau, Blue Book 2025).
  - Bedside echo assesses LV/RV, valves, effusion and congestion; normal EF does not exclude HFpEF or acute MR.

**Differential diagnosis of perioperative pulmonary oedema and acute dyspnoea with frothy secretions:**

| Diagnosis | Clues | Key action |
|---|---|---|
| Negative pressure pulmonary oedema | After laryngospasm or airway obstruction; young and fit; rapid onset | Relieve obstruction; oxygen with CPAP or PEEP; resolves in 12 to 48 h |
| Cardiogenic (LV failure, ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve lesion) | Cardiac history, hypertension, ECG change, raised troponin or BNP | Vasodilator, diuretic, treat ischaemia or rhythm |
| Fluid overload or TACO | Large positive balance, raised JVP, hypertension, responds to diuresis | Stop fluids, diuretic |
| Aspiration (gastric contents or blood) | Witnessed regurgitation or airway soiling; wheeze; focal infiltrate | Suction and supportive oxygenation/ventilation. Antibiotics are not routine for uncomplicated chemical pneumonitis; treat established/suspected infection appropriately. |
| Anaphylaxis | Hypotension, bronchospasm, rash, recent drug exposure | Adrenaline; fluid; stop trigger |
| TRALI | During/within 6 h of transfusion, hypoxaemia and bilateral oedema not primarily explained by LA hypertension; fever/hypotension may occur. BNP alone cannot reliably distinguish TRALI from TACO, especially in critical illness. | Stop transfusion, notify blood service, supportive lung-protective treatment. Diuretics are not routine for isolated TRALI but may be needed if hydrostatic overload coexists. |
| Pulmonary embolism | Sudden hypoxaemia, tachycardia, falling EtCO2 or widened PaCO2–EtCO2 gradient, RV strain; none is diagnostic alone. | Assess severity and bleeding; urgent PE team involvement for instability. Anticoagulation/reperfusion must account for recent surgery; see focused PE note below. |
| Bronchospasm or asthma | Wheeze, prolonged expiration, high peak pressures | Bronchodilators |
| Pneumothorax | Unilateral signs, hypotension, high airway pressure | Decompress |

Management follows the cause: secure the airway and oxygenation, apply CPAP or PEEP, obtain an ECG, troponin, chest X-ray or lung ultrasound, and treat the specific diagnosis.

## 5.3 Initial management (IT_RT 1.2, SS_IC 1.45)

### Preop

When pulmonary oedema is identified before surgery, stabilise oxygenation and haemodynamics, define the cause and defer elective surgery until decongested/optimised. Urgent surgery requires an agreed resuscitation and postoperative-care plan.

**Principles:** sit upright, oxygen titrated for hypoxaemia, early positive pressure when appropriate, vasodilator if BP permits, diuretic (if volume-overloaded), and treat the precipitant. Use the mnemonic of immediate steps: S it up, **O**xygen/CPAP, **N**itrate, **D**iuretic, **I**nvestigate, **T**reat cause (and the opioid is no longer favoured).

| Step | Details | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Position and oxygen | Sit upright if haemodynamics permit. Give oxygen for hypoxaemia and titrate; commonly 94–98%, 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure; ACS-specific guidance may cap oxygen-treated SpO2 at 96%. Reassess ABG and avoid unnecessary hyperoxia. |  |
| CPAP or NIV | CPAP 5 to 10 cmH2O or BiPAP (IPAP 10 to 15 / EPAP 5 to 8) reduces work of breathing, intubation rate and short-term mortality in some meta-analyses | 3CPO: faster symptomatic/physiological improvement, neutral mortality primary outcome. It found no significant difference between CPAP and NIPPV on death/intubation; this does not establish universal equivalence in all patients. |
| Vasodilator | GTN spray 400 micrograms SL, then infusion 10 to 200 micrograms/min if SBP above 110 (preload and afterload reduction, coronary dilation); sodium nitroprusside for hypertensive crisis | GTN effective in hypertensive acute HF; high-dose isosorbide dinitrate bolus with low-dose furosemide (Cotter) reduced intubation |
| Loop diuretic | Furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV (venodilatation first, diuresis in 15 to 30 min). Lower doses in diuretic-naive patients (20 to 40 mg); higher doses in chronic users | DOSE |
| Opioid | Do not give morphine routinely for pulmonary oedema/anxiety. Use titrated opioid for a separate strong indication such as severe pain or palliation, monitoring ventilation and BP; observational associations do not prove causation. |  |
| Treat precipitant | Ischaemia (reperfusion), arrhythmia (cardioversion), hypertension (vasodilator), valve emergencies (surgery), fluid overload (diuresis, dialysis), anaemia (transfuse) |  |
| Intubation | Hypoxaemia and exhaustion despite NIV, GCS reduction, shock, inability to protect the airway. Induce cautiously: pre-oxygenate with CPAP, ketamine or etomidate, vasopressor ready; PEEP up to 10 to 15 cmH2O reduces venous return and afterload |  |
| Inotropes and MCS | For hypotension, cold and wet profile (see Topic 3) |  |

### Intraop

**Intraoperative pulmonary oedema:**

- Call for help; 100% oxygen; check airway, tube position, ventilation and circuit (rule out airway problem, tube obstruction, endobronchial migration).
- Stop non-essential fluid loading and the causative infusion/transfusion if suspected; stop relevant irrigation and inform the surgeon. Assess whether surgery should be abbreviated. Continue necessary haemorrhage resuscitation or anaphylaxis fluid treatment, guided by the mechanism and haemodynamics.
- Titrate PEEP (often starting 5–10 cmH2O) and lung-protective ventilation to oxygenation, compliance and haemodynamics; higher pressure can worsen RV failure or hypotension.
  - Prolong expiration when airflow obstruction is present, rather than routinely for every oedema case.
  - Suction obstructing frothy secretions as needed without repeated derecruitment.
- Diagnose the type: ECG and ST analysis, arterial blood gas, ETCO2 (PE), lung ultrasound, TOE (RWMA, valve, LV function), look for anaphylaxis (bronchospasm, flushing, hypotension), transfusion reaction, or negative pressure.
- Treat: vasodilator (GTN) if hypertensive, diuretic if overloaded, inotrope if low output, antiarrhythmic or cardioversion, treat ischaemia, adrenaline if anaphylaxis.

### Postop

- Plan postoperative ICU/HDU, ventilation, and investigations (troponin, echo, BNP).

## Acute pulmonary embolism: crisis bridge (IT_RT 1.2)

- PE may resemble pulmonary oedema or cause perioperative collapse.
- Assess haemodynamics, RV function, biomarkers and bleeding risk; in stable patients use an appropriate diagnostic pathway/CTPA, while unstable patients may need bedside echo and immediate treatment decisions without unsafe transfer.
- Echo RV strain is supportive but not specific, and its absence does not exclude PE.
- Anticoagulate when indicated and safe; high-risk PE may require systemic thrombolysis, catheter treatment or surgical embolectomy, chosen with a PE response team, especially after recent surgery.
- Stabilise before interhospital transfer and consider locally available rescue.
- Source: AHA/ACC multisociety PE guideline 2026.

## 5.4 Special types

| Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (Type I: acute obstruction; Type II: chronic obstruction relieved) | Forced inspiration against an obstructed airway generates very negative intrapleural pressure (up to -100 cmH2O), increasing venous return and transmural capillary pressure, with sympathetic surge and hypoxia injuring capillaries. Treatment: relieve obstruction, O2, CPAP or PEEP; usually resolves in 12 to 24 h; diuretics seldom needed |
| TACO vs TRALI | TACO is hydrostatic overload; TRALI is permeability injury within 6 h and may coexist with other factors. BNP/JVP/BP support assessment but are not individually definitive. Stop transfusion, notify blood service and support oxygenation. Diurese TACO; avoid routine diuresis in isolated TRALI unless overload coexists. |
| Re-expansion pulmonary oedema | Risk follows rapid lung re-expansion after effusion or pneumothorax. For therapeutic pleural aspiration, BTS 2023 generally advises ≤1.5 L per attempt, slow drainage and stopping for symptoms; this volume rule does not apply identically to pneumothorax chest drainage. Avoid uncontrolled suction and treat supportively if oedema occurs. |
| Neurogenic pulmonary oedema | After acute neurological injury, sympathetic and permeability effects may contribute. Treat neurological cause and oxygenation/ventilation; alpha blockade is not a routine evidence-based standard and may compromise cerebral perfusion. |
| Pre-eclampsia, peripartum cardiomyopathy | Obstetrics sets |

## 5.5 Cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic oedema (SS_IC 1.45)

| Feature | Cardiogenic | Non-cardiogenic (ARDS) |
|---|---|---|
| History | Cardiac disease, ischaemia, volume overload | Sepsis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion |
| Heart size / vascular pedicle | May be enlarged, but acute MR/HFpEF can have normal heart size. | Often normal; pre-existing cardiomegaly can coexist. |
| Distribution on CXR | Often central/basal with effusions; substantial overlap. | Often patchy/diffuse; distribution alone is not diagnostic. |
| BNP | Often elevated; affected by age, renal function, rhythm and obesity. | Can be elevated in critical illness/RV strain; no definitive BNP boundary. |
| PAOP | Often elevated; no universal >18 criterion. | May be elevated with mixed disease; PAOP ≤18 is not required for ARDS. |
| Echo | LV systolic/diastolic dysfunction or valve pathology; preserved EF does not exclude it. | May be normal or show coexisting LV/RV dysfunction. |
| Oedema fluid protein : plasma protein | Historically lower in hydrostatic oedema; not a routine or universally validated bedside cut-off. | Historically higher with permeability injury; timing/mixed disease limit discrimination. |
| Response to diuretic and vasodilator | Prompt | Cause-dependent; conservative fluid management can still matter after stabilisation. |

items.title: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.body:
## 6.1 Classification

| Type | Key features | Perioperative priority |
|---|---|---|
| Dilated (DCM) | LV dilatation and systolic dysfunction not explained solely by abnormal loading or CAD; EF is reduced but <40% is not a universal diagnostic threshold. Genetic/familial, inflammatory, toxic, tachycardia-related and peripartum causes; exclude ischaemic/valve explanations. | Treat as HFrEF (Topic 3) |
| Hypertrophic (HCM) | Unexplained LVH (wall 15 mm or more), diastolic dysfunction, myocyte disarray; autosomal dominant sarcomere mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3); dynamic LVOT obstruction in about 70% (rest or provoked) with systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve; SCD risk | **Examiner favourite**; avoid anything that reduces LV size or increases contractility or heart rate |
| Restrictive (RCM) | Stiff ventricle, normal EF, biatrial enlargement; amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, fibrosis, radiation | Preload-dependent, fixed low output, poor tolerance of tachycardia and AF |
| Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy | RV fibrofatty replacement, VT | Arrhythmia risk; ICD |
| Takotsubo (stress) | Transient ventricular dysfunction after stress; multiple patterns, may coexist with CAD. Diagnose after excluding ACS and other causes. | Can occur intraoperatively; supportive care, avoid catecholamines if LVOT obstruction |
| Peripartum | Otherwise unexplained HF with EF <45% late in pregnancy or in postpartum months; exact historical time window is not an absolute boundary. | See obstetrics sets |
| Ischaemic | Not truly a primary cardiomyopathy (CAD) | Topics 1 to 3 |
| Right heart failure | RV pressure or volume overload (pulmonary hypertension, PE, RV infarct) | See 6.6 |

**Additional points from Cardiomyopathy and anaesthesia (Ibrahim and Sharma, BJA Education 2017):**

- **DCM:** a heterogeneous phenotype with genetic, inflammatory, toxic and other causes; ischaemic and valve disease should be distinguished from primary DCM.
  - Echo evaluates dilatation, EF, regional motion, MR, RV function and thrombus; reduced EF and fractional shortening indicate systolic dysfunction but no single FS or TAPSE threshold defines DCM.
  - Severe LV dysfunction, congestion, arrhythmia, fibrosis and poor functional status predict risk.
  - Do not anticoagulate solely because EF is <30% in sinus rhythm: indications include AF, documented thrombus, embolism or another established indication.
  - Anaesthetic aims remain avoidance of myocardial depression, tachycardia and abrupt afterload increase, euvolaemia and slowly titrated induction because circulation time may be prolonged.
  - Etomidate often causes relatively little haemodynamic change; ketamine can be useful in selected circumstances but may increase demand or depress a catecholamine-depleted heart.
  - Propofol lowers contractility and SVR; titrate carefully.
  - Neuraxial afterload reduction may help but hypotension must be prevented.
  - Select arterial/central monitoring, TOE and postoperative ICU according to severity and procedure.
- **HCM:** LVOT obstruction is a peak gradient ≥30 mmHg at rest or with physiological provocation; ≥50 mmHg is an important threshold for treatment decisions in symptomatic patients.
  - Approximately two-thirds may demonstrate obstruction at rest or with provocation, with proportions depending on the cohort and test.
  - AF is common and often poorly tolerated.
  - Sudden-death risk varies widely and is not uniformly ≥1% per year; use current risk assessment.
  - For hypotension from dynamic LVOTO, restore afterload with phenylephrine/vasopressin and correct true underfilling; avoid reflex fluid if congested and avoid inotropes that aggravate obstruction.
  - GA has not been proven universally safer than neuraxial anaesthesia; abrupt sympathectomy is the concern, so choose a controlled technique and monitoring.
- **RCM:** echo shows marked biatrial enlargement; the key diagnostic task is separating RCM from constrictive pericarditis (echo, CT, MRI, endomyocardial biopsy). Positive-pressure ventilation can reduce venous return enough to cause arrest; ketamine or etomidate are suitable agents.
- Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy may involve RV, LV or both.
  - Fibrofatty replacement, ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death can precede overt dysfunction.
  - Suspect with compatible family history, VT morphology, ECG abnormalities and exercise association; diagnosis integrates ECG, ambulatory rhythm, imaging, genetics and family assessment, with CMR important but not diagnostic alone.
  - Beta-blockers and selected antiarrhythmics (e.g. sotalol or amiodarone) are specialist treatments; verapamil is not a generic disease treatment.
  - Exercise counselling and individual ICD risk assessment are essential; not every patient automatically receives an early ICD.
- Peripartum cardiomyopathy has heterogeneous outcomes by region, phenotype and access to treatment; historical 30–60% mortality is not an appropriate contemporary universal estimate.
  - Severe LV dysfunction, RV involvement, thrombus, embolism and delayed diagnosis matter.
  - Both GA and carefully titrated neuraxial techniques have been used for caesarean delivery; technique, timing and monitoring depend on cardiac stability, anticoagulation and obstetric urgency.

## 6.2 Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

**Pathophysiology: asymmetric septal hypertrophy narrows the LV outflow tract. During systole, the Venturi effect and drag forces pull the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum (SAM), worsening obstruction and causing posterior-directed MR. Obstruction is dynamic:**

- It worsens with reduced LV volume (hypovolaemia, vasodilation), increased contractility (catecholamines, inotropes) and tachycardia, and reduced afterload.
- Diastolic dysfunction from LVH raises LVEDP, and myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch causes ischaemia despite normal coronaries.

| Factor | Increases obstruction | Decreases obstruction |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Hypovolaemia, venodilation, PEEP, positioning (head up) | Correct genuine underfilling with reassessed fluid; leg raise may help assess response. Avoid routine loading/head-down if congested or otherwise unsafe. |
| Afterload | Vasodilation, low SVR | Vasoconstrictors (phenylephrine, vasopressin) |
| Contractility | Beta agonism/inotropy and sympathetic stimulation may worsen LVOTO; correct clinically significant hypocalcaemia when needed rather than treating calcium as absolutely prohibited. | Beta-blockers, verapamil, volatile agents, disopyramide |
| Heart rate | Tachycardia (shortens diastolic filling and LV size) | Controlled rate without marked bradycardia; preserve sinus rhythm. |
| Rhythm | AF (loss of atrial kick, poor filling) | Sinus rhythm |

## 6.3 Dilated cardiomyopathy and low EF

Treat as severe LV systolic dysfunction (Topic 3), with attention to arrhythmia, devices and thromboembolism.

**Cardiac implantable devices (pacemaker, ICD, CRT) in cardiomyopathy:**

## 6.4 Restrictive cardiomyopathy and amyloidosis

- Stiff, non-compliant ventricles: small changes in volume cause large changes in pressure; fixed stroke volume depends on HR (avoid bradycardia); tolerate neither hypovolaemia nor fluid overload; AF is poorly tolerated.

## 6.6 Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension (supporting context; the BT_PO 1.5 right-heart-failure component is allocated to Set 12 in the current workbook)

**Aetiology:**

- Pulmonary hypertension (group 1 PAH; group 2 left heart disease; group 3 lung disease or hypoxia; group 4 CTEPH; group 5 multifactorial), RV infarction, PE, congenital shunt, cor pulmonale.
- PH is defined invasively by mean PAP >20 mmHg. Precapillary PH also requires PAWP ≤15 mmHg and PVR >2 Wood units; postcapillary PH has PAWP >15 mmHg, with PVR distinguishing isolated versus combined disease.
- Echo estimates probability and consequences but does not replace right-heart catheterisation when definitive classification is required.

**Pathophysiology:** the RV is a thin-walled, compliant, volume-tolerant pump poorly adapted to high afterload. A rise in PVR dilates the RV, flattens the septum (ventricular interdependence), reduces LV filling, and lowers RV coronary perfusion, causing a vicious spiral of ischaemia, further failure and shock.

items.title: Perioperative considerations: cardiac medical conditions
items.body:
Preop, intraop and postop considerations for the chronic cardiac medical conditions, in one place. Each section keeps its chapter number so you can jump back to the background in the chapter dropdown. Acute conditions (chapters 2 and 5) keep their anaesthetic sections inside their own dropdowns.

**Contents (section numbers):**

- **IHD and hypertension:** 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8
- **Heart failure:** 3.3, 3.5
- **Valve disease:** 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7
- **Cardiomyopathy:** 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5, 6.6

## IHD and hypertension · 1.2 Assessing severity, stability and risk

### Preop

The task is to define clinical stability, procedural urgency and cardiac risk, then choose appropriate optimisation, testing, monitoring and shared decision-making. Unstable disease generally warrants postponing elective surgery; elevated calculated risk alone does not automatically require delay or cardiology referral.

**Step 1:** Is there an active cardiac condition? Delay elective surgery for:

- Acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina
- Recent MI: highest risk early after the event, especially within 30 days. Timing depends on residual ischaemia, recovery, revascularisation, antiplatelet requirements and surgical urgency; a historical 60-day interval after MI without PCI is not a universal clearance threshold.
- Decompensated heart failure
- Significant arrhythmia (rapid AF, high-grade AV block, symptomatic VT)
- Severe symptomatic valve disease

**Step 2: Surgical risk.** Low (<1% MACE: cataract, endoscopy, breast), intermediate (1 to 5%: orthopaedic, intraperitoneal, carotid), high (>5%: open aortic and major vascular, emergency major laparotomy).

**Step 3: Functional capacity.** Metabolic equivalents (MET): 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min.

| Capacity | Examples |
|---|---|
| <4 METs (poor) | Limited everyday activity; stair-climbing questions are screening prompts and do not assign an exact MET value. Use DASI or objective testing selectively. |
| 4 to 7 METs | Moderate activities such as brisk level walking; individual energy expenditure varies. |
| >10 METs (excellent) | Sustained vigorous exercise, e.g. running or vigorous swimming; do not assign >10 MET solely from an activity name. |

DASI ≤34 and inability to climb two flights identify patients who merit closer risk assessment; neither is a stand-alone diagnosis or guarantee of an event. In the METS study, subjective assessment performed poorly while DASI predicted the primary death/MI outcome; natriuretic peptides have additional prognostic evidence.

**AHA/ACC 2024 perioperative guideline:**

- DASI above 34 is associated with lower risk, while inability to climb two flights is a useful warning sign rather than an exact MET measurement.
- Consider BNP/NT-proBNP and/or troponin in appropriately selected elevated-risk patients; CCS thresholds of BNP 92 ng/L and NT-proBNP 300 ng/L are perioperative risk thresholds, not universal diagnostic cut-offs.
- Normal biomarkers support proceeding without additional ischaemia testing when the whole clinical assessment is reassuring; they do not override new symptoms or active cardiac disease.
- Consider postoperative troponin surveillance in high-risk patients.
- Resting echo is indicated for new/worsening dyspnoea, suspected significant valve disease or a change in HF status; stable asymptomatic LV dysfunction does not need routine reassessment.
- A recent echo need not be repeated if the clinical state is unchanged, but new symptoms justify reassessment even within a year.
- Stress testing or coronary CT angiography is selective: poor/unknown capacity, elevated calculated risk and a result that would change management.

**Step 4: Risk indices.**

| Tool | Content |
|---|---|
| Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI, Lee 1999) | Six predictors: high-risk surgery (original definition: intraperitoneal, intrathoracic or suprainguinal vascular), IHD, HF, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine >177 micromol/L. One point each. Original major-cardiac-complication rates and contemporary death/MI/arrest rates are different endpoints; use a validated current calculator and specify population rather than applying one percentage series universally. RCRI omits important procedure, frailty and functional details. |
| NSQIP MICA / Gupta | Online calculators with more predictors (age, ASA, functional status, creatinine, procedure type) |
| Biomarkers | Preoperative BNP or NT-proBNP (CCS 2017 recommends for age 65 or over, RCRI 1 or more, or age 45 to 64 with cardiovascular disease). High risk if BNP 92 ng/L or more, or NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or more |

**Step 5: Further testing only if it changes management.**

| Test | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 12-lead ECG | Known cardiovascular disease or relevant symptoms before elevated-risk surgery; routine ECG is not indicated for asymptomatic low-risk procedures. | Baseline for postoperative comparison |
| Resting echo | Dyspnoea of unknown cause, known HF with change in status, suspected significant valve disease | Not routine |
| Stress testing (exercise ECG, dobutamine stress echo, perfusion scintigraphy) | Poor or unknown functional capacity AND elevated-risk surgery AND result would change management | See radionuclide imaging below |
| Coronary angiography | Only for standard indications (ACS, high-risk stress result) | Not for 'clearing' a patient |
| CT coronary angiography | Selective alternative in elevated-risk patients with poor/unknown capacity when identification of high-risk coronary anatomy would change management; not routine. | Not routine |

- **Radionuclide imaging.** Myocardial perfusion scintigraphy (thallium-201 or technetium-99m sestamibi with exercise or pharmacological stress using dipyridamole, adenosine or dobutamine) detects reversible perfusion defects.
- Strengths: high negative predictive value, quantifies ischaemic burden.
- Limitations: low positive predictive value, false positives from LBBB or attenuation artefact, and false negatives from balanced three-vessel disease, cost, and radiation.
- A large reversible defect or multiple affected territories predicts higher risk; thresholds depend on technique and cohort and are not independent indications for revascularisation.
- Dobutamine stress echo is an alternative that also provides valve and wall motion data; a new wall motion abnormality at a low workload predicts higher risk, with interpretation based on the complete study rather than a universal 60%-of-maximum-HR cut-off.

> **Pitfall:** there is no evidence that testing then revascularising reduces perioperative events in stable IHD (CARP; see trials; DECREASE-V is not relied on because of research-integrity concerns). Revascularise only for indications independent of the surgery.

## IHD and hypertension · 1.3 Recent MI and coronary stents

**Recent MI:**

- Defer elective surgery until the acute event has been treated and clinical stability established.
- Individualise the interval using symptoms, ventricular function, MI mechanism, PCI status and antithrombotic requirements.
- The historical recommendation to wait at least 60 days after MI without intervention is not proof that risk normalises at day 60.
