Contemporary observational NSTEMI data suggest 90–180 days may be reasonable after revascularisation, while risk can remain elevated without revascularisation; this is not a randomised timing rule.
- If surgery cannot wait, explain risk to patient and surgeon, involve cardiology, establish whether coronary treatment or DAPT is required, and plan invasive BP/ST monitoring, postoperative HDU and troponin surveillance.
- Apply the separate PCI timings below when relevant.

**Stent types and timing:**

| Stent | Antiplatelet duration | Earliest elective non-cardiac surgery (guideline guide; check current local advice) |
|---|---|---|
| Balloon angioplasty alone | Antiplatelet plan depends on indication and cardiologist; do not assume a universal 2–4-week DAPT course. | Delay elective non-cardiac surgery at least 14 days. |
| Bare-metal stent (BMS) | DAPT at least 1 month | At least 30 days if antiplatelet interruption is needed; do not interrupt within 30 days unless an overriding emergency dictates. |
| Drug-eluting stent (DES), stable disease | DAPT 6 months (shorter in high-bleeding-risk patients) | At least 6 months; 3 months only if the delay is harmful |
| DES after ACS | Default ACS DAPT about 12 months; individualised shorter regimens for bleeding risk. | At least 12 months for elective surgery requiring interruption. Selected time-sensitive surgery may be considered ≥3 months after DES if delay is more harmful, with MDT planning. |

**Mechanisms:**

- Stent thrombosis is the dreaded complication (often catastrophic; reported mortality varies by cohort and era).
- Early premature DAPT cessation is the strongest predictor.
- Surgery is prothrombotic (catecholamines, inflammation, platelet activation, rebound after antiplatelet withdrawal).
- Newer-generation DES have faster endothelialisation, so shorter DAPT courses are now accepted.

**Stent thrombosis risk factors:**

- Recent ACS, previous stent thrombosis on therapy, complex left main/bifurcation PCI, multiple or overlapping stents, residual dissection or malapposition, poorly controlled diabetes, severe renal dysfunction and impaired LV function.
- Restenosis (neointimal growth/recurrent narrowing) and thrombosis (acute thrombotic occlusion) are different problems.
- Historical BMS and first-generation DES event rates should not be extrapolated to contemporary DES; modern DES reduce restenosis and generally have better safety than BMS.
- DAPT duration depends on ACS versus chronic disease, bleeding risk, PCI complexity and the cardiologist’s plan.
- AHA/ACC 2024: surgery requiring antiplatelet interruption within 30 days of any stent is harmful; continue DAPT when possible within 30 days of BMS or 3 months of DES.
- After DES for ACS, defer elective surgery requiring interruption for at least 12 months; after DES for chronic coronary disease, at least 6 months is reasonable.
- Selected time-sensitive surgery may proceed at 3 months if delaying it poses greater risk.

- **Mechanism and duration of clopidogrel.** Prodrug;
- Absorbed, then about 85% is hydrolysed by esterases to inactive metabolite;
- The remaining 15% is activated by hepatic CYP2C19 (and CYP3A4/2B6) to an active thiol metabolite that **irreversibly** binds P2Y12 on the platelet.
- Platelet inhibition therefore lasts the platelet lifespan (7 to 10 days); platelet function recovers at about 10% per day from new platelet production.
- Loss-of-function CYP2C19 variants reduce effect; PPIs (omeprazole) may interfere via CYP2C19.

| P2Y12 inhibitor | Reversibility | Stop before surgery | Neuraxial block (ASRA/ESRA guide) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clopidogrel | Irreversible | 5 to 7 days | 5 to 7 days |
| Prasugrel | Irreversible, more potent | 7–10 days (AHA/ACC recovery interval; local protocols may use 7). | 7 to 10 days |
| Ticagrelor | Reversible, direct acting | 3–5 days; separate surgical and neuraxial recommendations. | 5 days (ASRA fifth edition 2025). |
| Cangrelor (IV) | Reversible, half-life about 3 to 6 min | Bridging option; stop 1 to 6 h before | At least 3 h after stopping before needle placement; catheter removal and restart require the ASRA-specific plan (first dose ≥8 h after removal). |

**Perioperative antiplatelet strategy:**

- Elective surgery: defer until the minimum DAPT period is complete.
- If surgery cannot be deferred, **continue low-dose aspirin** after PCI if possible, balancing stent thrombosis against procedural bleeding risk.
  - Intracranial, spinal canal and selected ophthalmic procedures may require interruption.
  - Long-term antithrombotic treatment is individualised: some patients are on P2Y12 monotherapy or an anticoagulant-based regimen, so do not automatically add aspirin or assume every stented patient takes it lifelong.
- Stop the P2Y12 inhibitor at the appropriate interval only after a joint surgeon–cardiologist–anaesthetist decision. Restart as soon as surgical haemostasis permits, often within 24–48 hours; timing and any loading dose must account for bleeding risk, the drug, PCI indication and an indwelling neuraxial catheter.
- For exceptional patients with very high thrombotic risk when surgery cannot be deferred, specialist intravenous antiplatelet bridging (usually cangrelor) may be considered.
  - This is not routine, evidence in non-cardiac surgery is limited, and neuraxial timing must be planned.
  - Heparin does not replace platelet inhibition for prevention of stent thrombosis.
- For high-risk surgery soon after PCI or when antiplatelet interruption is unavoidable in a high-risk stent, choose a centre with rapid access to interventional cardiology and an agreed rescue plan; a 24-hour cath lab is particularly relevant in these cases.
- If surgery proceeds on DAPT, plan haemorrhage management and access to blood products.
  - Platelet transfusion is considered for significant bleeding rather than prophylactically in every patient.
  - Circulating ticagrelor can inhibit transfused platelets, so early transfusion may be ineffective; clopidogrel/prasugrel active metabolites are shorter-lived and transfusion is more effective after drug clearance.
  - Seek haematology advice; platelet-count correction does not demonstrate restored platelet function.

## IHD and hypertension · 1.4 Perioperative drug therapy in IHD

| Drug | Recommendation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Beta-blocker | Continue chronic therapy unless contraindicated by shock/bradycardia. If newly indicated, start optimally >7 days before surgery and titrate to tolerance; do not begin high-dose therapy on the day. | POISE: fewer MIs but more deaths and strokes with high fixed-dose metoprolol, from hypotension and bradycardia. DECREASE trials unreliable (data integrity concerns) |
| Statin | Continue; start in vascular surgery or if indicated | Withdrawal increases events; low risk |
| Aspirin | After PCI continue aspirin if possible, balancing thrombosis and bleeding. Secondary prevention without PCI is individualised. Do not start for primary prevention before surgery. | POISE-2: no reduction in death or MI, more major bleeding |
| Clonidine | Do not start; continue only if chronically taking (rebound) | POISE-2: no benefit; more hypotension, non-fatal cardiac arrest |
| ACE inhibitor / ARB | Individualise by indication, BP, HF and local policy: AHA/ACC 2024 permits omission 24 h before elevated-risk surgery in selected hypertensive patients; continuing in HFrEF is reasonable. AOA/BIHS 2026 generally recommends continuing, including day of surgery. | STOP-or-NOT: 22% composite complications in both groups; intraop hypotension 54% continuation vs 41% discontinuation. No single policy is proven superior for every patient. |
| Nitrates | Continue; avoid abrupt cessation | Rebound angina |
| Calcium channel blockers | Continue |  |
| Anticoagulants | Per indication (see valve section for mechanical valves) | CHEST 2022 |

**AHA/ACC 2024 additions:**

- If a beta-blocker is newly indicated, start sufficiently early to assess tolerance and titrate, optimally more than 7 days before surgery.
- Withhold SGLT2 inhibitors 3 to 4 days before surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin).
- For primary prevention, stop aspirin and do not start it preoperatively; if aspirin must be stopped, hold it 4 to 5 days.
- Bridging with heparin for warfarin is only for high thrombotic risk, and DOACs need no bridging.
- Consider delaying elective surgery if BP is 180/110 mmHg or above before the day of surgery; intraoperatively keep MAP at or above 60 to 65 mmHg (SBP 90 mmHg or more) and treat postoperative MAP below 60 or SBP below 90 mmHg promptly.
- BP postponement thresholds differ: the 2026 Association of Anaesthetists/BIHS guideline uses clinic BP ≥180/120 mmHg and generally continues ACEi/ARB, whereas AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission 24 h beforehand in selected hypertensive patients having elevated-risk surgery.
- Record the chosen local approach and drug indication.

## IHD and hypertension · 1.5 Intraoperative management of IHD

### Intraop

**Haemodynamic goals:**

- Avoid tachycardia and marked bradycardia; use the patient’s usual rate, ventricular function and ischaemia to set an individual target rather than an obligatory 50–80/min.
- Maintain coronary perfusion and avoid sustained MAP below 60–65 mmHg or SBP below 90 mmHg; a higher target may be needed in selected patients.
- A percentage of baseline is a guide, not a trial-proven universal target.
- Maintain adequate preload without overload and preserve contractility.
- Give oxygen for hypoxaemia, avoiding unnecessary hyperoxia.
- Correct anaemia according to bleeding, symptoms and ischaemia: a liberal strategy toward Hb 100 g/L may be reasonable in ACS with anaemia (MINT; AHA/ACC 2025), but is not a mandatory threshold for every patient.
- In stable cardiovascular disease, about 80 g/L is a commonly considered transfusion threshold, modified by clinical context.
- Avoid hypothermia, shivering, hypercapnia and pain.

**Anaesthetic technique:** no technique is shown to be superior. Use volatile agents (modest ischaemic preconditioning, still debated), TIVA or balanced anaesthesia. Regional anaesthesia gives sympathetic block with reduced HR but can cause hypotension with neuraxial block; thoracic epidural may improve myocardial supply-demand but is not routinely indicated.

**Detection of ischaemia: ECG monitoring and other methods.**

| Method | Sensitivity and notes |
|---|---|
| 5-lead ECG with ST analysis | Historical selected study (London et al., 1988): V5 ~75%, II+V5 ~80%, V4+V5 ~90%, II/V4/V5 ~96% of detected episodes; these are not universal clinical sensitivity estimates. Choose lead placement for likely territory. Diagnostic/ST mode with appropriate filtering reduces artefact; verify monitor-specific settings rather than assuming one filter applies to every device. |
| ST criteria | For formal acute ischaemia use a diagnostic 12-lead ECG: new horizontal/downsloping ST depression ≥0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads; J-point elevation ≥1 mm except V2–V3 (men ≥40: ≥2 mm; men <40: ≥2.5 mm; women: ≥1.5 mm), in the absence of confounding LVH/BBB. Monitor ST-trend alarm thresholds differ. New LBBB alone is not diagnostic of acute occlusion. |
| Limitations | LBBB, LVH with strain, paced rhythm, digoxin, WPW, electrolytes and hypothermia impair interpretation. ECG misses ischaemia in territories not covered (posterior, inferior in lead II only) and most ischaemia is silent under GA |
| TOE | New RWMA can precede ECG change and is useful during instability, but is not specific for ischaemia and may be chronic, load-related or paced. Requires skilled interpretation and comparison; not routine for every non-cardiac case. |
| PA catheter | Rising PAOP, large v waves (ischaemic MR); poor sensitivity |
| Invasive BP and haemodynamics | Hypotension or rising filling pressures are late signs |
| Troponin | Selected postoperative surveillance, commonly at 24/48 h or daily for 48–72 h depending on guideline and risk; interpret baseline and assay. |

**Treatment of intraoperative ischaemia:**

- Correct the trigger first (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxaemia, pain, light anaesthesia), then use nitrate (GTN infusion if BP allows), a short-acting beta-blocker (esmolol) for tachycardia with adequate BP, phenylephrine or noradrenaline to restore coronary perfusion pressure, and 12-lead ECG.
- Call cardiology early for ST elevation (cath lab), see Topic 2.

## IHD and hypertension · 1.6 Postoperative: troponin surveillance, MINS and risk reduction

### Postop

- Most MINS is asymptomatic and occurs in the first 48–72 h.
  - Select patients for surveillance using guideline-specific criteria: CCS recommends daily troponin for 48–72 h in defined higher-risk groups;
  - ESC uses preoperative and 24/48 h hs-troponin in selected patients;
  - AHA/ACC 2024 states postoperative surveillance may be reasonable in high-risk patients.
  - These are not identical universal day-1-to-3 protocols.
- MINS defined (VISION): high-sensitivity troponin T 20 to under 65 ng/L with an absolute rise of 5 ng/L or more, or 65 ng/L or more.
  - Diagnosis of MINS needs no ischaemic symptoms.
  - These VISION thresholds refer to the Roche hs-troponin T assay and study population, not every troponin assay.
  - Exclude a clear non-ischaemic cause and consider the preoperative baseline; MINS and MI are not interchangeable.
- Management: assess urgently for ongoing ischaemia, acute coronary occlusion, haemodynamic instability and non-ischaemic injury.
  - Correct triggers (anaemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypoxaemia, hypotension, infection) and arrange cardiology review and cardiovascular prevention.
  - Statin and antiplatelet treatment depend on the mechanism, CAD indication and surgical bleeding risk; aspirin is not automatic for every postoperative troponin rise.
  - Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily may be considered for selected MINS patients with low bleeding risk after haemostasis, suitable renal function and no contraindication (MANAGE); high discontinuation and trial limitations matter.
  - It is not immediate routine treatment for all MINS.
- Care environment: HDU or monitored bed for high-risk patients; analgesia (multimodal, avoid NSAID in IHD and renal disease), avoid hypothermia, shivering, anaemia, hypotension.

## IHD and hypertension · 1.7 Chronic hypertension (IT_PO 1.4)

### Preop

**Definition and grades (Australian/ISH):**

- Clinic BP 140/90 mmHg or more; grade 1 140 to 159 / 90 to 99; grade 2 160 to 179 / 100 to 109; grade 3 180 or more / 110 or more.
- More than 90% is essential hypertension; secondary causes to consider: renal parenchymal disease and renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism (hypokalaemia), phaeochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation, OSA, drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, OCP, stimulants).
- Use the higher category when systolic and diastolic grades differ, confirm with repeated correctly measured readings and home/ambulatory BP, and distinguish these chronic diagnostic thresholds from perioperative postponement thresholds.

**Consequences relevant to anaesthesia:**

- Left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction: poorly tolerates tachycardia, AF and hypovolaemia; very sensitive to preload.
- Longstanding hypertension may shift organ autoregulatory limits and is associated with vascular disease; the magnitude varies and cannot be inferred from a single clinic reading. Avoid prolonged hypotension, using usual BP, organ perfusion and comorbidity to individualise the target.
- Exaggerated hypotension at induction and exaggerated pressor response to laryngoscopy and surgical stimulation.
- Associated IHD, CKD, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure, AF, aortic dilatation.

**Perioperative risk and when to delay:**

| BP | Action |
|---|---|
| Confirm correctly measured BP; below the applicable local postponement threshold. | Usually proceed if no acute organ injury or unstable disease. Optimise long-term control; do not rapidly normalise an isolated clinic reading. |
| Severe confirmed elevation or suspected acute target-organ injury. | AHA/ACC 2024: consider deferral with ≥180/110 in selected elevated-risk elective cases. AOA/BIHS 2026: clinic ≥180/120 or home/ambulatory ≥175/115 prompts review/deferral. Acute organ injury requires urgent assessment; urgent surgery needs a joint risk-based plan. |

**Antihypertensive drugs:**

| Drug class | Perioperative approach |
|---|---|
| Beta-blockers | Continue (withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and ischaemia) |
| Calcium channel blockers | Continue |
| Clonidine / methyldopa | Continue chronic central agents; clonidine withdrawal particularly risks rebound hypertension. Methyldopa is not identical to clonidine and context matters. |
| ACE inhibitor / ARB | Individualise by indication, BP, HF and local policy: AHA/ACC 2024 permits omission 24 h before elevated-risk surgery in selected hypertensive patients; continuing in HFrEF is reasonable. AOA/BIHS 2026 generally recommends continuing, including day of surgery. Restart promptly when perfusion/renal function permit. |
| Diuretics | Assess congestion, renal function, potassium and fasting/volume status. Omission may suit a euvolaemic hypertensive patient; continue/adjust when needed for HF congestion rather than universally withholding. |
| Aldosterone antagonists | Check potassium |

### Intraop

**Intraoperative:**

- Minimise hypotension and large BP swings.
- Treat sustained MAP below 60–65 mmHg or SBP below 90 mmHg promptly and individualise a higher target when indicated.
- POISE-3 compared bundled MAP ≥80 versus ≥60 mmHg strategies plus different antihypertensive policies and found no difference in vascular outcomes; it did not validate a universal “within 20% of baseline” rule.
- Blunt excessive laryngoscopy responses with appropriately titrated opioid, esmolol or anaesthetic depth.
- Treat induction vasodilation with vasopressor; give fluid when there is evidence of hypovolaemia or responsiveness rather than reflex large boluses.

**Severe perioperative hypertension:**

- First check the measurement and treat pain, light anaesthesia, hypercapnia, hypoxaemia, bladder distension, fluid overload and drug withdrawal.
- Hypertensive emergency means acute target-organ injury, not a BP number or nonspecific symptoms alone.
- Use titratable IV treatment matched to the organ injury (labetalol, GTN, esmolol, nicardipine or clevidipine; hydralazine has a less predictable response).
- In most emergencies reduce MAP by no more than about 20–25% in the first hour, then gradually; aortic dissection, stroke, ACS and pregnancy have specific targets.
- Severe asymptomatic BP elevation usually requires gradual oral adjustment and follow-up rather than rapid IV normalisation.

### Postop

Monitor for hypotension, hypertension, myocardial injury and AKI; treat pain, hypoxia and volume imbalance. Resume the agreed antihypertensive regimen when haemodynamically stable, and arrange follow-up for newly identified or poorly controlled hypertension.

## IHD and hypertension · 1.8 Peripheral vascular disease: perioperative bridge (IT_PO 1.4)

### Preop

PVD is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis; assess CAD, cerebral/renal disease, functional limitation, limb perfusion, diabetes, renal function, antithrombotic indication and urgency. In acute limb ischaemia, record sensory/motor deficit and urgent vascular input; do not delay limb-saving treatment for routine coronary testing. Optimise statin and cardiovascular prevention.

### Intraop

Preserve systemic and limb perfusion, avoid sustained hypotension, hypoxaemia, hypothermia and major anaemia. Plan vascular access away from diseased/infected sites and account for anticoagulation before neuraxial/regional procedures. With reperfusion anticipate acidosis, hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia and haemodynamic change.

### Postop

Monitor limb perfusion, compartment syndrome, reperfusion metabolic disturbance, bleeding, AKI and myocardial injury; restart indicated antithrombotics when haemostasis permits and continue prevention, mobilisation and vascular follow-up.

## Heart failure · 3.3 Perioperative assessment of LV function and filling status (SS_CS 1.4)

### Preop

**Clinical:** orthopnoea, PND, oedema, JVP, S3 gallop, crepitations, hepatomegaly, ascites, cool peripheries, exercise tolerance (NYHA, DASI).

**Investigations:**

| Test | Value |
|---|---|
| BNP / NT-proBNP | Acute dyspnoea: BNP <100 ng/L or NT-proBNP <300 makes acute HF less likely, with exceptions (especially obesity/flash oedema). Non-acute thresholds differ (e.g. BNP <35/NT-proBNP <125 in older ESC pathways). Age, AF and renal dysfunction raise values; obesity suppresses them. Perioperative risk thresholds are different again. |
| ECG | Ischaemia, LBBB (dyssynchrony), AF, LVH, QRS duration for CRT |
| CXR | Cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, effusions |
| Echo | LVEF (biplane Simpson), regional wall motion, valves, filling pressures, RV function, pulmonary pressures |
| Cardiac MRI, nuclear | Viability, aetiology, EF |
| Invasive | PA catheter data for complex cases |

**Echo assessment of LV systolic function:**

| Parameter | Normal / cut-off |
|---|---|
| LVEF (ASE) | 52 to 72% men, 54 to 74% women; mildly reduced 41 to 51 / 41 to 53 |
| Fractional shortening | Method-, sex- and geometry-dependent; approximately high-20s to mid-40s percent in standard adult references. Regional dysfunction or abnormal geometry reduces reliability; do not use one FS value to define HF. |
| Global longitudinal strain | Approximately −18 to −20% or more negative in many systems; vendor, load, age and method matter. Adds sensitivity to longitudinal dysfunction but is not universally a superior replacement for EF. |
| Fractional area change (mid-papillary SAX) | LV mid-papillary FAC is a qualitative/semiquantitative adjunct with no universal 35% normal threshold. FAC ≥35% is the commonly used RV area-change reference; do not transfer it to the LV. |
| Qualitative on FoCUS | Normal, mildly, moderately or severely reduced; interventricular septum motion |
| Dimensions | LVIDd 3.8–5.2 cm women; 4.2–5.8 cm men (ASE 2015); interpret indexed size and image plane. |

- **Echo assessment of diastolic function: use the 2025 ASE update, which supersedes the 2016 four-variable algorithm.** Integrate mitral inflow, annular e′ velocities, E/e′ and TR velocity/PASP; use LA volume and reservoir strain and other supplementary measures to adjudicate discordant findings.
- Average E/e′ >14, TR velocity >2.8 m/s and LAVI >34 mL/m² support elevated filling pressure in the appropriate setting, but no single value diagnoses HFpEF.
- Age, rhythm, significant valve disease, pacing and loading conditions require modified interpretation.
- The table below retains the teaching patterns, not a stand-alone diagnostic algorithm.

| Teaching pattern | E/A | E/e' | Other | Typical pressure context; integrate 2025 algorithm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal pattern | Age/rate dependent; may be 0.8–2 | Usually low | Normal e′/LA structure support interpretation | Usually normal; inflow alone is insufficient |
| I impaired relaxation | Often <0.8 | Not necessarily elevated | Reduced e′; low E supports low/normal LAP | Usually normal at rest; pressure may rise with exercise |
| II pseudonormal | Often 0.8–2 | Often elevated, not a mandatory 10–14 band | Reduced e′ plus LA/TR/strain evidence; Valsalva may help | Elevated when integrated criteria support it |
| III restrictive | Often ≥2 | Often >14 | Short DT; interpret rhythm, valve disease and loading | Usually elevated, but E/A alone does not grade every patient |

- **Assessment of filling status versus fluid responsiveness (see Set 10): these are different questions.** CVP, PAOP, IVC size/collapse and E/e′ may inform pressure/congestion but do not reliably predict a useful stroke-volume response to fluid.
- Passive leg raise with real-time LVOT VTI or cardiac-output measurement is useful when feasible.
- PPV/SVV require appropriate controlled ventilation, regular rhythm and assessment of tidal-volume, lung compliance, RV function and other limitations; use predicted body weight and do not increase ventilation injuriously merely to obtain an index.
- In spontaneously breathing adults, IVC ≤2.1 cm with >50% inspiratory collapse supports RAP about 3 mmHg, with important exceptions.
- In HF, any fluid challenge should be small and immediately reassessed; stop if congestion develops.

## Heart failure · 3.5 Anaesthetic implications and perioperative risk (IT_PO 1.4)

### Preop

HF is a major independent predictor of perioperative mortality, MACE, readmission and prolonged stay. Elective surgery should be deferred if decompensated; optimise euvolaemia and GDMT beforehand.

### Intraop

**Haemodynamic goals:**

| Systolic dysfunction | Diastolic dysfunction |
|---|---|
| Preload: maintain but avoid overload | Preload: maintain, adequate filling is crucial |
| Afterload: avoid excessive resistance while preserving organ/coronary perfusion; titrated vasopressor may be needed. | Afterload: avoid large rises |
| Rate: individualise; avoid both tachycardia/ischaemia and output-limiting bradycardia. Do not force high-normal HR in all HFrEF. | Rate: avoid tachycardia and allow filling; excessive bradycardia also reduces output. No mandatory 50–80/min range. |
| Rhythm: keep sinus rhythm | **Sinus rhythm is critical**; treat AF early (cardioversion if unstable) |
| Contractility: support with inotrope if needed; avoid negative inotropes | Contractility: preserved; avoid excess inotropy |
| Avoid hypoxaemia, hypotension, fluid overload, ischaemia and unnecessary myocardial depression. | Avoid tachycardia, ischaemia, hypervolaemia |

**Anaesthetic technique:**

- Choose agents with minimal myocardial depression: etomidate or ketamine (with caution) or slow-titrated propofol for induction; opioid-based, balanced technique; volatile agents are acceptable at low MAC.
- Invasive arterial monitoring before induction for severe LV dysfunction; consider cardiac output monitoring and TOE.
- Vasopressor (noradrenaline) infusion ready before induction; inotrope (dobutamine, adrenaline) or milrinone if low output; vasopressin for vasodilatory states.
- Neuraxial anaesthesia can be well tolerated in compensated HF (controlled onset, slow titration of epidural or CSE; sympathetic block reduces afterload) but severe aortic stenosis or fixed output states are an exception.
  - Maintain MAP with vasopressors.
  - Monitor ECG, SpO2 and blood pressure (arterial line for severe dysfunction), and watch for signs of fluid overload or pulmonary oedema throughout.
- Fluids: individualised and goal-directed; avoid large crystalloid loads; treat blood loss with blood.

### Postop

- Postoperative: choose ward, HDU or ICU according to disease severity and surgical stress; extubate when stable, provide effective analgesia, monitor fluid balance, renal function, potassium and congestion, and restart HF therapy promptly when safe.
  - Use troponin surveillance in selected high-risk patients; repeat BNP or echo for a clinical question rather than routinely in every case.
  - Restart SGLT2 inhibitor only when eating/drinking, haemodynamically stable and free of ketosis.

## Valve disease · 4.3 Aortic stenosis (most examinable)

### Preop

- If severe symptomatic AS requires urgent non-cardiac surgery, balloon aortic valvuloplasty or TAVI may be considered as a bridge (see trials).

**Valve treatment:**

- Heart Team selection of SAVR versus TAVI uses age, life expectancy, anatomy, access, surgical risk, associated coronary/aortic disease and lifetime reintervention strategy.
- ESC/EACTS 2025 generally recommends TAVI from age 70 in suitable tricuspid AS with appropriate anatomy, and SAVR in younger low-risk patients; age alone is insufficient.
- PARTNER 3 and other trials support TAVI in selected low-risk patients, not every anatomy.
- Mechanical versus bioprosthetic choice affects anticoagulation and future management.

**ESC/EACTS 2025 changes:**

- Early intervention should be considered as an alternative to surveillance for selected asymptomatic severe high-gradient AS at low procedural risk; intervention is recommended with LVEF <50% without another cause.
- In mixed AS/AR, symptoms plus Vmax ≥4 m/s or mean gradient ≥40 mmHg support intervention.
- TAVI generally uses single antiplatelet therapy when there is no other anticoagulation/PCI indication.
- Mechanical valves require lifelong VKA with valve- and patient-specific INR targets.
- TEER is recommended for carefully selected symptomatic severe ventricular secondary MR despite optimised HF treatment/CRT; EF <50% alone is not an indication.
- In primary MR, symptoms, LV dysfunction and cardiac-damage markers guide repair.
- In severe AR, class I surgical triggers include symptoms or significant LV dysfunction/dilatation; earlier surgery may be considered in low-risk asymptomatic patients with LVEF ≤55%, LVESDi >22 mm/m² or LVESVi >45 mL/m².
- These earlier thresholds are not interchangeable with the strongest class I triggers.
- Consult the full 2025 recommendation tables for anatomy and eligibility.
- For asymptomatic severe AR, the stronger surgical triggers include LVEF ≤50%, LVESD >50 mm or LVESDi >25 mm/m²; the earlier 55%/22 mm/m²/45 mL/m² thresholds concern selected low-risk intervention decisions.

### Intraop

- Avoid the three killers: hypotension, tachycardia and loss of effective atrial contribution.
  - Preserve sinus rhythm when feasible, avoid marked bradycardia, and individualise a low-normal rate (often about 60–80/min as a teaching guide).
  - Maintain coronary perfusion and an appropriate baseline-related BP; 65 mmHg may be insufficient in some patients.
  - Aim for euvolaemia, replacing demonstrable deficits without routine “slightly full” loading.
- Vasopressor first (phenylephrine, metaraminol, noradrenaline) at induction and during neuraxial block; avoid pure vasodilators. Pre-emptive vasopressor infusion.
- Defibrillator pads on; use synchronised cardioversion for haemodynamically unstable AF/SVT; manage stable arrhythmia according to rate, symptoms and thromboembolic considerations.
- GA with controlled induction and slow titration; avoid spinal single-shot block (rapid sympathectomy); slow epidural or CSE and low-dose spinal with infusion of vasopressors have been used in selected cases.
- Invasive arterial line before induction; consider TOE for major surgery.

### Postop

- Postoperative HDU.

## Valve disease · 4.4 Aortic regurgitation

### Preop

For AR, define acute versus chronic disease, symptoms, LV size/function, aortic root pathology and surgical indication. Acute severe AR or decompensation needs urgent specialist treatment; assess whether valve/aortic intervention should precede elective non-cardiac surgery.

### Intraop

**Anaesthetic goals:**

- Avoid marked bradycardia; a high-normal rate may be appropriate (**80–100**/min is an illustrative guide, adjusted for ischaemia and ventricular function) (shortens diastole, reducing regurgitant time), avoid bradycardia (increases regurgitant volume per beat), maintain preload, **reduce SVR** (vasodilators help), maintain contractility.
- Avoid IABP (contraindicated).

### Postop

Monitor congestion, perfusion and rhythm; avoid bradycardia and abrupt afterload increases, restart appropriate therapy and use HDU/ICU for severe disease or major surgery.

## Valve disease · 4.5 Mitral stenosis

### Preop

| Issue | Approach |
|---|---|
| Severity | Echo (mean gradient, MVA, PASP), symptoms (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, embolism). Severe symptomatic MS should be treated (balloon valvotomy or surgery) before elective surgery |
| Rate and rhythm | Continue beta-blocker or diltiazem/digoxin for rate control; avoid premedication that causes anxiety and tachycardia. AF with rapid ventricular response: cardiovert if unstable; beta-blocker or amiodarone; avoid pure inotropes |
| Anticoagulation | VKA for rheumatic moderate/severe MS with AF or LA thrombus (not DOAC). Bridging is individualised by thrombotic/bleeding risk; do not state that CHEST 2022 mandates bridging. |

### Intraop

| Issue | Approach |
|---|---|
| Preload | Maintain; avoid fluid overload (small increments) |
| PVR | Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, nitrous oxide, lung hyperinflation; the RV must not fail |
| SVR | Maintain; avoid vasodilatation (neuraxial block with caution) |
| Pneumoperitoneum | Raised intrathoracic pressure, reduced venous return, CO2 absorption increasing PVR, steep head-down raises LA pressure; use low insufflation pressure (10 to 12 mmHg) and gentle positioning. This patient may be better off with open or regional/field technique depending on severity |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, large-bore access, CVP or PAC are of limited value (PCWP overestimates LVEDP in MS), TOE |
| Drugs | Avoid unnecessary tachycardia from drugs; titrate induction/opioid to haemodynamics. Reversal follows neuromuscular monitoring, drug and renal status; sugammadex may avoid antimuscarinic tachycardia but has no established universal outcome superiority in MS. |

### Postop

| Issue | Approach |
|---|---|
| Postoperative | HDU; analgesia; early extubation with careful reversal |

**MS in pregnancy (Holmes, BJA Education 2017):**

- Pregnancy often unmasks MS because cardiac output rises about 50%; worse than moderate disease (MVA below 1.5 cm2) commonly gives heart failure in the second or third trimester.
- Control tachycardia and AF aggressively with beta-blockers, add diuretics for congestion, and use percutaneous commissurotomy if medical therapy fails because it avoids bypass.
- For delivery, place neuraxial analgesia early, establish it slowly, treat hypotension with alpha-agonists, and assist the second stage; consider caesarean section in pulmonary hypertension or NYHA III/IV symptoms.
- Flash pulmonary oedema can follow delivery from decompression of the IVC and autotransfusion (head-up, oxygen initially for severe hypoxaemia then titrated to target, CPAP/PEEP and intubation if needed).
- Give oxytocin with great care (systemic vasodilation, raised PVR) and avoid ergometrine, which is contraindicated.
- Use a pregnancy heart team and current 2025 ESC pregnancy guidance; delivery mode, assisted second stage and anticoagulation require an individual plan rather than an automatic rule.

## Valve disease · 4.6 Mitral regurgitation

### Preop

- **Primary (degenerative: prolapse, flail, endocarditis, rheumatic) vs secondary (functional: LV dilatation, ischaemic).** Severity depends on the loading conditions, so interpret intraoperative regurgitation with BP, volume state and the awake baseline; general anaesthesia may underestimate MR.
- Chronic severe MR leads to LA dilatation (large compliance) and AF, then pulmonary hypertension.

**Assessment: define the mechanism (Carpentier type I normal motion with annular dilation or perforation, II prolapse or flail, IIIa restricted in systole and diastole, IIIb restricted in systole), severity by an integrated approach (EROA, regurgitant volume, vena contracta, pulmonary vein flow reversal), and the consequences: LV size and function, LA size, rhythm (AF), PASP and RV function. In chronic severe MR the LV ejects into a low-pressure LA, which flatters the ejection fraction:**

- An EF of 60% or less, or an end-systolic diameter of 40 mm or more, already signals LV dysfunction.
- BNP and exercise tolerance help detect decompensation.

### Intraop

**Haemodynamic goals:**

| Variable | Goal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Maintain; avoid both hypovolaemia and overload | Regurgitant volume depends on LA and LV filling |
| Heart rate | Avoid bradycardia; normal/high-normal according to LV function and ischaemia. | MR is systolic: avoid prolonged filling/large LV volume and excessive resistance to forward ejection. “Shorter diastole reduces regurgitation” is principally AR physiology, not a direct MR mechanism. |
| Afterload | Keep SVR low to normal | Vasoconstriction increases regurgitant fraction; vasodilators promote forward flow |
| Contractility | Maintain or support | Maintain forward output; after valve correction, loss of the low-impedance LA outlet can unmask afterload mismatch. |
| Rhythm | Rate-control AF; keep sinus rhythm where possible | Loss of atrial contribution reduces filling |
| Pulmonary vascular resistance | Keep low | Pulmonary hypertension from chronic LA hypertension threatens RV function |

**Pulmonary hypertension and RV protection in MR:**

- Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain and excessive airway pressures.
- Titrate PEEP to oxygenation and RV loading; do not abandon useful PEEP.
- Maintain systemic perfusion and RV coronary driving pressure with noradrenaline or vasopressin when needed, rather than treating SBP >PASP as an absolute target.
- Inhaled nitric oxide/epoprostenol or an inodilator may help selected RV failure, but in group 2 pulmonary hypertension from high LA pressure, pulmonary vasodilation can worsen oedema; first address LV/valve disease and use specialist monitoring.

**Technique and monitoring:**

- Either general anaesthesia (opioid-based balanced technique; avoid agents that cause bradycardia or marked myocardial depression) or a carefully titrated neuraxial or regional technique are acceptable; neuraxial block reduces afterload and is usually well tolerated in MR, unlike in stenotic lesions.
- Arterial line, large-bore access and ECG with ST analysis; TOE for major surgery and for any instability, because intraoperative loading conditions change the degree of regurgitation (and ischaemic or functional MR is dynamic).
- Treat intraoperative hypotension by correcting its mechanism: titrated noradrenaline or vasopressin can restore perfusion but both raise SVR, so avoid unnecessary vasoconstriction and add inotropy only for demonstrated low output; avoid bradycardia.
- Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture, endocarditis, chordal rupture) presents with pulmonary oedema and shock and requires urgent Heart Team/cardiac surgical assessment.
  - Use afterload reduction only if BP permits, vasoactive support and selected IABP/MCS as a bridge; hypotensive shock cannot be treated with unqualified nitroprusside.

### Postop

**MR points from Holmes, BJA Education 2017, interpreted with current guidance:**

- The posteromedial papillary muscle commonly has a single supply from the PDA, making it vulnerable after inferior MI; LCx runs close to the mitral annulus and is at risk during surgery.
- Chronic severe MR can mask systolic dysfunction: LVEF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm is an intervention trigger in primary MR.
- Asymptomatic severe MR with preserved LV function often permits non-cardiac surgery with appropriate monitoring, but does not confer zero additional risk.
- “Full, fast, forward” means euvolaemia, avoidance of bradycardia and excessive afterload, not liberal fluid or forced tachycardia.
- After repair/replacement, loss of the low-impedance regurgitant outlet can unmask LV dysfunction and require inotropic/afterload management; IABP is continued only when clinically indicated.
- In pregnancy, MR is often tolerated when LV function is preserved; delivery and second-stage assistance are individualised.

## Valve disease · 4.7 Prosthetic valves and anticoagulation

### Preop

- Mechanical-valve anticoagulation: first decide whether interruption is needed; minor low-bleeding-risk procedures may continue VKA at a therapeutic INR.
- If interrupted, stop warfarin about 5 days before surgery and check INR.
- Bridging is not automatic: CHEST 2022 suggests against routine bridging even for mechanical valves, while AHA/ACC 2024 and valve guidance allow it for selected very high thrombotic risk (e.g. mechanical mitral/older valve, recent embolism or valve thrombosis).
- Agree a valve-specific plan with cardiology/haematology.
- Bileaflet aortic valve without additional risk usually needs no bridge.
- BRIDGE excluded mechanical valves and cannot settle this question.
- When a therapeutic heparin bridge is chosen, start as INR becomes subtherapeutic;
- Stop therapeutic LMWH at least 24 h before surgery/neuraxial placement, longer or with testing in relevant renal impairment;
- Stop IV UFH 4–6 h before and confirm coagulation recovery.
- For neuraxial insertion, ASRA requires INR normalised to the local laboratory range, rather than a universal “<1.4”.

### Intraop

**Emergency reversal:**

- Life-threatening bleeding or urgent major surgery generally requires four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K (commonly 5–10 mg for major bleeding, per local protocol), not a routine 1–2 mg dose.
- PCC is dosed by INR, weight and product protocol (often 25–50 IU/kg with product-specific maxima); repeat INR and assess haemostasis.
- Low-dose vitamin K may suit non-bleeding elevated INR when time permits, but inadequate reversal must not be accepted simply to ease re-warfarinisation.
- FFP is an alternative when PCC is unavailable or specifically indicated.

### Postop

After surgery, restart warfarin when haemostasis and oral intake permit (often within 12–24 h). If therapeutic bridging is indicated, restart only after adequate haemostasis—often ≥24 h for lower bleeding risk and 48–72 h for high risk—and satisfy neuraxial catheter rules. Monitor INR, bleeding, embolism and valve function; resume full protection with an agreed specialist plan.

**Mechanical heart valves in pregnancy:**

### Preop

- Pregnancy is a high-risk anticoagulation decision requiring a pregnancy heart team.
  - VKA provides effective maternal mechanical-valve protection but causes dose-related embryopathy/fetal bleeding risks; no VKA dose is proven safe for the fetus.
  - Heparins do not cross the placenta, but inadequate LMWH dosing increases valve thrombosis.
  - If LMWH is selected, use twice-daily adjusted dosing and frequent anti-Xa monitoring.
  - ESC 2025 recommends individually agreed peak targets generally 1.0–1.2 IU/mL (4–6 h after dosing), with its dosing table giving 0.8–1.2; consider valve type/position and specialist protocol.
  - Trough >0.6 IU/mL has been proposed for selected higher-risk cases, but evidence is limited and this is not a universally established target.

### Intraop

- Options include carefully counselled VKA regimens (low-dose requirements reduce but do not eliminate fetal risk) or monitored heparin during the embryopathy window and near planned delivery, with timing set by the current pregnancy guideline and valve risk.
  - A common strategy replaces VKA near 36 weeks with monitored LMWH/UFH;**planned delivery** on therapeutic VKA is avoided.
  - For neuraxial placement, wait at least 24 h after therapeutic LMWH, or 4–6 h after IV UFH with normal coagulation; renal impairment can require longer.
  - Postpartum prophylactic and therapeutic restart intervals differ: therapeutic LMWH is generally delayed at least 24 h after lower-bleeding-risk surgery and 48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk surgery, with additional obstetric and catheter constraints.
  - Do not universally restart therapeutic heparin at 6–12 h.
  - ASRA therapeutic LMWH requires catheter removal ≥4 h before the first dose and the first dose ≥24 h after needle/catheter placement.
  - Warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding and may restart when haemostasis permits, with bridging only if indicated.

### Postop

- Delivery planning with a multidisciplinary team (cardiology, obstetrics, anaesthesia, haematology) and avoid delivery on warfarin (fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk, preference for caesarean if on warfarin).
  - Postpartum fluid shifts, haemorrhage, anaemia and thrombosis require monitored care and a documented anticoagulant/catheter restart plan; maintain specialist follow-up after discharge.

## Cardiomyopathy · 6.2 Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

### Preop

**Preoperative assessment:**

- Symptoms (dyspnoea, angina, syncope, palpitation), family history of sudden death, ECG (LVH, strain, deep Q waves), echo (wall thickness, LVOT gradient at rest and with Valsalva, SAM, MR, diastolic function), cardiac MRI (fibrosis, late gadolinium enhancement), Holter monitoring, and review of medications (beta-blocker, verapamil, disopyramide, amiodarone).
- An ICD requires a perioperative device plan, with magnet or reprogramming only when indicated (see Set 12).
- Current SCD assessment includes previous arrest/sustained VT, family history, massive LVH ≥30 mm, suspected arrhythmic syncope, apical aneurysm, LVEF <50%, NSVT and extensive LGE.
- LVOT gradient and other factors enter some risk models; gradient ≥30 mmHg or an abnormal exercise BP response alone is not an automatic ICD indication (AHA/ACC HCM 2024).

### Intraop

**Perioperative haemodynamic goals:**

- **Preload:** maintain euvolaemia and avoid fasting-related dehydration, venodilation and blood loss. Replace demonstrable deficit with small reassessed fluid or blood increments; do not prescribe “full” preload, routine IV maintenance for every fasting patient or indiscriminate fluid loading in a stiff congested ventricle.
- **Afterload:** preserve systemic pressure; phenylephrine or vasopressin is often preferred for hypotension with LVOTO. Noradrenaline may be needed for vasodilatory shock but its beta effect can aggravate dynamic obstruction, so titrate with echo and the clinical response.
- **Contractility:** reduce (volatile anaesthetics, beta-blocker).
- **Rate:** low-normal (often 60–70/min as a teaching guide, individualised), sinus rhythm (cardiovert early for AF; consider amiodarone).
- **Avoid:** ephedrine, adrenaline, dobutamine, isoprenaline, ketamine, tachycardia, hypovolaemia, and nitrates.

**Technique:**

| Element | Approach |
|---|---|
| Premedication | Continue beta-blocker or verapamil; anxiolysis (reduce catecholamines) |
| Monitoring | Arterial line before induction, ECG with ST, TOE if major surgery or instability, defibrillator pads, CVP of limited value |
| Induction | Slow titrated induction with opioid; have phenylephrine/vasopressin immediately available and start a titrated infusion when warranted by obstruction, BP and procedure, not automatically for every patient. |
| Maintenance | Volatile agent, opioid, remifentanil; avoid light anaesthesia and pain |
| Neuraxial | Choose a controlled technique. Abrupt sympathectomy from single-shot spinal may be poorly tolerated in severe obstruction; incremental epidural or carefully selected low-dose techniques can be used with monitoring and vasopressor support. No robust evidence proves GA universally safer. |
| Hypotension post induction | **Check cause and use echo early for refractory hypotension. If LVOTO: resto**re afterload with phenylephrine (e.g. 50–100 microgram titrated bolus) or vasopressin (not an alpha agonist), correct underfilling only if present, reduce excessive anaesthetic vasodilation and avoid beta-agonist inotropy. Cautious esmolol may help severe tachycardic LVOTO after pressure is supported and expert assessment; do not reflexively beta-block undifferentiated shock. Also exclude bleeding, anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, ischaemia and arrhythmia. |
| Pneumoperitoneum (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) | Pneumoperitoneum and head-up position can reduce venous return and raise airway pressure/PVR; higher SVR is not invariably beneficial. Use slow low-pressure insufflation, cautious positioning and volume guided by response rather than routine head-down/fluid loading. |
| Arrhythmia | Cardiovert unstable; amiodarone or beta-blocker for AF; do not use digoxin |
| Emergence | Avoid hypertension and tachycardia; extubate smoothly; ICU or HDU postoperative |

### Postop

Maintain smooth emergence, analgesia, oxygenation and sinus rhythm; avoid dehydration, fluid overload and tachycardia. Monitor for recurrent LVOTO, AF, myocardial injury and congestion. Use HDU/ICU for severe obstruction or major surgery and resume medication when safe.

**Pregnancy, labour and delivery in HCM:**

- Pregnancy changes that help: rising blood volume (40 to 50%) increases preload and enlarges the LV cavity, reducing the gradient.
- Changes that harm: falling SVR (more LVOT gradient), tachycardia and pain in labour, catecholamine surges, blood loss at delivery, and aortocaval compression.
- Principles: left lateral position, early slow-titrated epidural with a vasopressor ready, individualised second-stage assistance when needed (avoid prolonged haemodynamically stressful Valsalva), slow oxytocin infusion rather than a bolus (hypotension, tachycardia), avoid beta-agonist tocolytics where possible (tachycardia); select any tocolytic with the obstetric/cardiac team, and prompt volume replacement of haemorrhage.

- Alcohol septal ablation, myectomy, mavacamten (EXPLORER-HCM) and ICD are the disease treatments: myectomy for refractory obstruction; mavacamten (cardiac myosin inhibitor) reduces gradient and improves functional class.
- Mavacamten can depress EF and has major drug interactions: specialist prescribing and serial echo are required.
- It is contraindicated in pregnancy; preconception discontinuation follows the current product label and specialist plan.

## Cardiomyopathy · 6.3 Dilated cardiomyopathy and low EF

### Preop

- **Preop device assessment:** identify device/model, indication, pacing dependence, battery and lead status, programmed modes and magnet response.
  - Review a recent interrogation/remote transmission and obtain an updated assessment if status, symptoms or procedure requires it; AHA 2024 notes interrogation within about 3 months can inform dependence and function.
  - Historical 12-month pacemaker/6-month ICD intervals are not sufficient for every patient.
  - Echo/biomarkers address a clinical change, not the device alone.

### Intraop

- **Electromagnetic interference:** monopolar diathermy above the umbilicus is the main risk. Use bipolar diathermy or short bursts, place the return pad so the current path avoids the generator, and monitor the pulse waveform (pulse oximeter or arterial line) because the ECG may be distorted.
- **Pacemaker:** a magnet usually produces asynchronous pacing; reprogram to asynchronous mode if the patient is pacemaker-dependent and interference is expected.
  - Magnet behaviour is manufacturer-, programming- and battery-dependent; some leadless devices do not respond.
  - Confirm the response rather than assuming asynchronous pacing.
- **ICD:** a magnet usually suspends tachyarrhythmia therapies but does not alter pacing.
  - Suspend therapies (magnet or programmer) when clinically relevant EMI is expected, particularly monopolar diathermy above the umbilicus/near the generator, apply external defibrillation pads first, and have an external defibrillator ready.
  - Restore therapies and re-interrogate before the patient leaves a monitored area.
- **CRT:** loss of biventricular capture reduces cardiac output; confirm capture and treat AF or ectopy that reduces pacing percentage.

**Choosing the anaesthetic technique in severe LV dysfunction:**

| Technique | Advantages | Risks and precautions |
|---|---|---|
| Regional or neuraxial (slow epidural, CSE with incremental local anaesthetic, peripheral nerve block) | Avoids airway instrumentation and positive pressure ventilation; reduces afterload; allows titrated onset | Hypotension from vasodilation (have a vasopressor infusion running, titrate slowly), fluid overload from preloading, and anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy limiting neuraxial use. Single-shot spinal gives abrupt sympathectomy and is riskier |
| General anaesthesia | Controlled airway and ventilation; suits instability, pulmonary oedema or failed block | Loss of sympathetic tone, myocardial depression with induction agents, pressor response to laryngoscopy, reduced venous return with positive pressure ventilation; use titrated induction with arterial monitoring |
| Sedation or local | Minimal haemodynamic disturbance for superficial surgery | Over-sedation with hypoventilation raises PVR and CO2; maintain monitoring |

### Postop

Restore ICD therapies and any temporary device programming before leaving a monitored setting, with interrogation after reprogramming, major events or suspected malfunction. Follow the HF postoperative plan: assess output/congestion, renal function, electrolytes and rhythm; restart therapy safely.

**Alcohol and thiamine:** alcohol cardiomyopathy may improve with abstinence; give thiamine.

- Anthracycline cardiotoxicity is dose-related but can occur well below 450–550 mg/m²; contemporary cardio-oncology risk assessment recognises cumulative doxorubicin-equivalent exposure around ≥250 mg/m² plus patient factors as important.
- Trastuzumab has a distinct mechanism and risk profile, amplified by anthracycline exposure.
- Assess symptoms, prior therapy, current echo including strain when indicated, and biomarkers according to risk; do not use one dose threshold to exclude toxicity.

## Cardiomyopathy · 6.4 Restrictive cardiomyopathy and amyloidosis

### Preop

- Amyloid (AL, ATTR): autonomic hypotension, conduction disease, increased wall thickness with relatively low ECG voltage and poor tolerance of vasodilation are important.
  - Non-dihydropyridine CCBs are often poorly tolerated; digoxin is not an absolute contraindication in every patient but requires specialist indication, cautious dosing and close renal/level monitoring.
  - Identify subtype and disease therapy, arrhythmia, anticoagulation and extracardiac involvement before anaesthesia.

### Intraop

- Goals: maintain preload and sinus rhythm, avoid bradycardia and vasodilation, titrate anaesthetic, and use vasopressors (phenylephrine, vasopressin).

### Postop

Monitor rhythm/conduction, BP, renal function and congestion; maintain careful fluid balance and early access to pacing/vasopressor support when indicated. Use monitored postoperative care according to severity and surgical stress.

## Cardiomyopathy · 6.5 Takotsubo and peripartum cardiomyopathy

### Preop

Identify active/recent cardiomyopathy, recovery status, LVOTO, thrombus and HF; defer elective surgery during active decompensation and agree timing with cardiology. Pregnancy/postpartum cases need a pregnancy heart team.

**Takotsubo:**

- Often postmenopausal women after physical or emotional stress (including surgery), mimicking ACS with ECG change and troponin elevation.
- Apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis is common but other patterns occur, and significant CAD can coexist.
- Exclude acute coronary occlusion and myocarditis appropriately.
- LVOTO occurs in a subset and changes shock treatment: avoid inotropy/vasodilation that worsens obstruction; restore perfusion and address true underfilling.
- Without LVOTO, treat pump failure using tailored support and consider MCS for refractory shock.
- Anticoagulate documented LV thrombus and consider severe apical akinesis individually.
- EF often recovers over weeks, but complications and persistent symptoms occur.

**Peripartum cardiomyopathy:**

- Otherwise unexplained HF with LVEF <45% towards the end of pregnancy or in the postpartum months; the historical last-month-to-5-month window is useful but not an absolute modern boundary.
- Use pregnancy-compatible HF treatment (selected beta-blocker, hydralazine/nitrate and diuretic as indicated); avoid ACEi/ARB/ARNI, SGLT2 inhibitors and contraindicated drugs during pregnancy.
- Postpartum treatment considers breastfeeding.
- Anticoagulate for thrombus, AF or embolism and consider severe LV dysfunction according to guideline-specific thresholds (often EF <30–35%) and bleeding risk; it is not automatic at one EF value.
- Bromocriptine is a selected specialist option, suppresses lactation and requires at least prophylactic anticoagulation.
- Plan delivery and prolonged postpartum observation with a pregnancy heart team.

### Intraop

Use carefully titrated anaesthesia, invasive pressure monitoring when indicated, echo for instability, and phenotype-specific support: distinguish LVOTO from primary pump failure. Avoid major sympathetic surges and excess fluid; manage anticoagulation according to bleeding and neuraxial timing.

### Postop

Plan monitored recovery for significant disease, with attention to fluid shifts, recurrent HF, arrhythmia, thromboembolism and safe medication restart; continue cardiac follow-up even when EF improves.

## Cardiomyopathy · 6.6 Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension (supporting context; the BT_PO 1.5 right-heart-failure component is allocated to Set 12 in the current workbook)

### Preop

Define PH group, functional class, recent decompensation, RV function, oxygen requirement and established pulmonary vasodilators. Involve PH/cardiology services for significant disease, avoid interruption of continuous prostacyclin and plan rescue therapy and postoperative destination.

**Management principles (perioperative RV failure):**

### Intraop

| Principle | Actions |
|---|---|
| Preload | Euvolaemia; avoid overload and underfilling. CVP trend plus echo/perfusion informs management, but 8–12 mmHg is not a universal target. Decongest when overloaded. |
| Afterload (PVR) | Avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis and excessive lung distension; titrate PEEP to recruitment and RV loading rather than avoiding all PEEP. Continue established PAH therapies. Inhaled NO/epoprostenol can rescue selected RV failure; systemic pulmonary vasodilators require specialist indication and may worsen group 2 HF oedema. |
| Contractility | Dobutamine, milrinone, low-dose adrenaline; levosimendan |
| Perfusion pressure | Maintain systemic pressure and RV coronary driving pressure relative to RV/RAP and diastolic pressures. Noradrenaline/vasopressin are titrated to perfusion; SBP >PASP is not an absolute target. |
| Rhythm | Maintain sinus rhythm; cardiovert early |
| Mechanical | RVAD, VA-ECMO, atrial septostomy in selected |
| Anaesthetic | Avoid anything that increases PVR (nitrous oxide, N2O, ketamine in large doses, hypoventilation); neuraxial anaesthesia with care; aim for PVR down and SVR up |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, CVP, PA catheter or TOE (RV size, septal position, TAPSE, FAC) |

### Postop

Continue oxygen/PAH treatment and monitor perfusion, rhythm, analgesia, ventilation and fluid balance. Avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, pain and abrupt withdrawal of vasodilators; selected patients need ICU because RV failure may emerge after surgery or extubation.

**Echo of RV function:**

- TAPSE below 17 mm, S' below 9.5 cm/s, FAC below 35%, RV:LV ratio above 1, septal flattening (D-sign), and PASP from TR velocity (PASP = 4 x v^2 + RAP).
- These indices are load- and angle-dependent and must be integrated.
- TR-derived RVSP approximates PASP only without significant RV outflow/pulmonary valve obstruction and with a reliable TR envelope/RAP estimate.

items.title: 7. Heart and great vessel anatomy for ultrasound imaging
items.body:
## 7.1 Cardiac chambers and valves

| Structure | Key anatomy | Echo relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Right atrium | Receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus; crista terminalis; Eustachian valve; right atrial appendage | Venous return and RAP assessment; CVC tip usually lower SVC/cavoatrial region according to device/local policy, not unqualified deep RA placement. Pacing leads cross to the appropriate chamber. |
| Right ventricle | Most anterior chamber, crescentic in cross-section, trabeculated with moderator band; tricuspid valve (3 leaflets: anterior, septal, posterior) at a slightly more apical position than the mitral | RV size and function (TAPSE, S', FAC) |
| Left atrium | Posterior, receives four pulmonary veins; left atrial appendage (LAA) is a common site for thrombus | TOE assesses LAA thrombus before cardioversion in the appropriate pathway; a negative examination does not eliminate all embolic risk or replace indicated anticoagulation. |
| Left ventricle | Thick-walled, bullet-shaped; two papillary muscles (anterolateral: dual supply; posteromedial: single supply from PDA); smooth septum | EF, wall motion, wall thickness |
| Interatrial septum | Fossa ovalis (patent foramen ovale in about 25%) | Bubble study; PFO and paradoxical embolism |
| Aortic valve | Tricuspid; right, left and non-coronary cusps; right and left coronary ostia arise from their sinuses | Short-axis 'Mercedes-Benz' sign; cusp morphology |
| Mitral valve | Anterior (aortic) and posterior leaflets; scallops P1 to P3 and A1 to A3; annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles | Mechanism of regurgitation; SAM in HCM |
| Pulmonary valve | Tricuspid, anterior and superior to the aortic valve | Gradient, PR |
| Pericardium | Fibrous and serous layers; 15 to 50 mL of fluid | Effusion/tamponade: RA collapse typically systolic and RV free-wall collapse early diastolic; integrate Doppler, chamber pressures and clinical findings. |

**Valve relationships:** the aortic and mitral valves are in fibrous continuity (the aorto-mitral curtain), which is why the LVOT is important in SAM and in AV endocarditis extension. The tricuspid is more apical than the mitral (normal offset varies with imaging plane and body size; it is not uniformly 10 mm). The pulmonary valve is the most anterior and cephalad valve.

## 7.2 Coronary arteries

| Vessel | Origin and course | Supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Left main | Left sinus of Valsalva; bifurcates after 1 to 2 cm | LAD and LCx |
| LAD | Anterior interventricular groove to the apex | Anterior LV wall, anterior two-thirds of septum, apex, anterolateral papillary muscle (partly) |
| LCx | AV groove, posterior | Lateral LV wall, posterior wall in left-dominant circulation, SA node in 40% |
| RCA | Right sinus of Valsalva, right AV groove | RA, RV, inferior LV wall, posterior third of septum (via PDA in right dominance, 85%), SA node in 60% and AV node in 90% |
| PDA | From RCA (right dominant 85%), LCx (left dominant 8%) or both | Inferior septum, posteromedial papillary muscle |

**Venous drainage:**

- Coronary sinus (great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein) drains to the RA; thebesian veins drain directly into the chambers.
- Anaesthetic relevance: the coronary sinus is cannulated for retrograde cardioplegia, and the great cardiac vein accompanies the anterior interventricular/LAD region and curves into the left AV groove near LCx; a fixed close relationship to the left main should not be assumed.

**17-segment AHA/ASE model:** divides the LV into basal (6), mid (6), apical (4) and apex (1); apical and septal segments are LAD, inferolateral and anterolateral usually LCx, and inferior RCA or PDA. Use it to map RWMA to coronary territories. Coronary dominance, wrap-around LAD and overlapping supply vary, so a segmental map suggests rather than proves the culprit artery.

## 7.3 Great vessels

| Vessel | Anatomy | Echo and anaesthetic relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Ascending aorta | Aortic root and ascending aorta to brachiocephalic origin; normal diameter depends on age, sex and body size rather than a universal 3.7 cm. | Dissection (type A), aneurysm; TOE blind spot at the distal ascending aorta |
| Aortic arch | Brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian arteries | Cannulation and cerebral perfusion in arch surgery; suprasternal view |
| Descending thoracic aorta | Usually left/posterolateral to the oesophagus and posterior to the LA; spatial relation varies along its course. | TOE views (excellent); atheroma grading; IABP tip sits 1 to 2 cm distal to the left subclavian |
| Pulmonary trunk and arteries | Trunk divides into right and left PAs; ligamentum arteriosum | PAC passes through RA, RV and PA; wedge pressure; saddle PE |
| SVC | Formed by brachiocephalic veins; drains to RA with the azygos entering above | CVC tip location: cavo-atrial junction |
| IVC | Enters the RA from below; hepatic veins join below the diaphragm | Subcostal view: IVC diameter and collapsibility |
| Pulmonary veins | Four veins to the LA | Pulsed Doppler (pulmonary vein flow for MR and diastolic function); AF ablation |
| Coronary sinus | Posterior AV groove into the RA | Cardioplegia and CRT lead placement |

## 7.4 Transthoracic windows and standard views

| Window | Views | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Parasternal (left, 3rd to 4th intercostal space) | Long axis (PLAX): RV, septum, LV, LVOT, aortic valve, mitral valve, LA, descending aorta behind LA. Short axis (PSAX): aortic valve level (Mercedes-Benz sign), mitral level ('fish mouth'), papillary muscle level ('doughnut' for LV wall motion) | LV size, EF, valve morphology, effusion, RV pressure overload (D-shaped septum) |
| Apical (cardiac apex) | 4-chamber, 5-chamber (adds LVOT and aortic valve), 2-chamber, 3-chamber (apical LAX) | Chamber sizes, MV and TV, TAPSE, Doppler gradients (CW alignment) |
| Subcostal | 4-chamber, IVC and hepatic vein view | Useful for effusion/RV/LV and IVC assessment when windows permit. During arrest, acquire within planned rhythm checks without prolonging compression pauses; IVC size/collapse alone does not establish volume responsiveness. |
| Suprasternal | Aortic arch | Arch and descending aorta, coarctation |

**Focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) questions:** Is there pericardial fluid or tamponade? Is LV function grossly normal, reduced or hyperdynamic? Is the RV dilated (RV:LV above 1)? Is the IVC plethoric? Is there a gross valve lesion? Is there a regional wall motion abnormality?

## 7.5 Transoesophageal views (ASE/SCA basic perioperative TOE)

- The oesophagus lies posterior to the left atrium.
- The probe's position is described as upper oesophageal (UE), mid-oesophageal (ME), transgastric (TG) and deep transgastric.
- The ASE/SCA basic perioperative examination comprises 11 views; the 2013 comprehensive examination has 28 (the older 20-view set was comprehensive, not basic).
- The following is a selected teaching list, not the complete basic protocol.
- Common; the examiner favourites are:

| View | Angle | Key structures |
|---|---|---|
| ME four-chamber | 0 to 20 degrees | All four chambers, MV and TV, LV lateral and septal walls, RV function |
| ME two-chamber | 80 to 100 | LA, LAA, MV, LV anterior and inferior walls |
| ME long axis | 120 to 160 | LVOT, aortic valve, MV, LA, proximal ascending aorta (anteroseptal and posterior walls) |
| ME aortic valve short axis | 30 to 60 | Aortic valve cusps, coronary ostia |
| ME bicaval | 90 to 110 | SVC, IVC, RA, LA and interatrial septum, RAA (catheter position and PFO) |
| ME RV inflow-outflow | 50 to 70 | TV, RVOT, PV, pulmonary artery |
| TG mid short axis | 0 | Mid-LV circumferential wall motion from several coronary territories; useful for continuous comparison but misses basal/apical disease and is not a complete ischaemia examination. LV cavity size is not a direct filling-pressure measurement. |
| Descending aortic short and long axis | 0 and 90 | Atheroma, dissection flap, IABP position |
| Deep TG long axis | 0 to 20 | LVOT and aortic valve alignment for Doppler gradients |
| UE aortic arch | 0 and 90 | Arch branches |

**Normal adult reference values (ASE chamber quantification 2015, interpreted with contemporary RV guidance):**

- LVIDd 3.8–5.2 cm in women and 4.2–5.8 cm in men; septal/posterior wall thickness about 0.6–0.9 cm in women and 0.6–1.0 cm in men; LVEF 54–74% in women and 52–72% in men; RV basal diameter ≤4.1 cm and TAPSE ≥17 mm are common reference points.
- Prefer indexed LA volume (upper reference 34 mL/m²) to one anteroposterior diameter.
- Aortic root size depends on age, sex and body size; 3.7 cm is not a universal upper limit.
- Typical native AV area 3–4 cm² and MV area 4–6 cm².
- IVC ≤2.1 cm alone is not a complete RAP assessment.
- PASP and RV indices require clinical context; use current ASE 2025 RV guidance rather than treating 35 mmHg as an absolute normal/abnormal boundary.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
**Evidence check:**

- The trial results below were checked against primary publication abstracts/results and linked records in November 2026. Sample sizes, endpoints, follow-up intervals and important limitations are specified; neutral primary outcomes are not presented as proof of equivalence.
- Trial names link to the intended publication, with separate links for separately reported factorial components.

## 8.1 Perioperative risk and cardiac protection (Topic 1)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [POISE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18479744/) (Lancet 2008) | RCT, 8,351 patients, non-cardiac surgery; metoprolol CR 100 mg pre-op then 200 mg daily vs placebo | 30 d: composite CV death/MI/arrest 5.8% vs 6.9%; all MI 4.2% vs 5.7% (the old 3.6/5.1 figures were not all MI). Death 3.1% vs 2.3%; stroke 1.0% vs 0.5%. | Do not start high-dose beta-blocker on the day of surgery; continue chronic therapy | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [POISE-2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24679062/) (NEJM 2014) | 2×2 factorial RCT, 10,010 patients; aspirin and clonidine comparisons reported separately. | Aspirin death/nonfatal MI 7.0% vs 7.1%; major bleeding 4.6% vs 3.8%. Clonidine: no primary benefit; important hypotension 47.6% vs 37.1%, nonfatal arrest 0.3% vs 0.1%. | Do not initiate aspirin/clonidine solely for surgical protection. Recent stents were not adequately represented: PCI antiplatelet decisions require guideline-specific assessment. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [POISE-2 clonidine report (NEJM 2014)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24679061/) | Separate clonidine component of the same 10,010-patient factorial trial. | No reduction in death/nonfatal MI; important hypotension 47.6% vs 37.1%, nonfatal arrest 0.3% vs 0.1%. | Do not initiate clonidine for surgical cardioprotection; chronic withdrawal is a different issue. | Primary abstract/results checked. |
| [POISE-3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35363452/) (NEJM 2022) | POISE-3 TXA: 9,535 randomised; 1 g IV at start and end of non-cardiac surgery. BP component separately published in Ann Intern Med 2023. | 30 d composite bleeding 9.1% vs 11.7% (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.87). CV composite 14.2% vs 13.9%; prespecified noninferiority not established (upper one-sided CI 1.14 exceeded 1.125 margin). | TXA reduces bleeding in major surgery; BP management has no simple trial-proven target | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [POISE-3 BP strategy (Ann Intern Med 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37094336/) | 7,490 treated hypertensive patients; MAP ≥80/medication-withholding bundle vs MAP ≥60/continuation bundle. | 30 d vascular death/nonfatal MINS/stroke/arrest 13.9% vs 14.0% (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.88–1.12). Adherence incomplete. | No benefit demonstrated for the higher-MAP bundle; cannot isolate a single BP target or medication effect. | Primary abstract/results checked. |
| [CARP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15625331/) (NEJM 2004) | RCT, 510 patients with stable CAD before vascular surgery; revascularisation vs none | 510 randomised; at median 2.7 y mortality 22% vs 23% (P=.92); postoperative MI 12% vs 14% (P=.37). | No routine prophylactic revascularisation in stable CAD solely for vascular surgery. Excluded important groups such as significant left-main disease; standard independent revascularisation indications still apply. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [VISION troponin cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28444280/) (JAMA 2017) | Prospective cohort, 21,842 adults ≥45 undergoing inpatient non-cardiac surgery; Roche hsTnT. | 30 d mortality by peak hsTnT: 20–<65 ng/L 3.0%; 65–<1000 9.1%; ≥1000 29.6%. MINS 17.9%, of whom 93.1% lacked ischaemic symptoms. Observational association; assay-specific thresholds. | Supports prognostic use of surveillance in selected patients. Does not by itself prove that screening or a particular treatment improves outcomes. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [MANAGE report](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29900874/) (Lancet 2018) | 1,754 patients within 35 d of MINS; dabigatran 110 mg twice daily vs placebo, up to 2 y. | Major vascular complications 11% vs 15% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.93); safety bleeding composite 3% vs 4% (HR 0.92, CI 0.55–1.53), not significantly different. | Selected patients after haemostasis/renal assessment. Limitations include early termination, high discontinuation (46% vs 43%) and selected population; nonsignificant bleeding result does not prove no bleeding risk. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [STOP-or-NOT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39212270/) (JAMA 2024) | 2,222 patients; RASI continuation vs discontinuation 48 h before major non-cardiac surgery. | 28 d death/major complications 22% in each group (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.19); intraoperative hypotension 54% continuation vs 41% discontinuation. | Either approach acceptable; withholding is reasonable in hypertensive patients | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [METS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30070222/) (Lancet 2018) | Prospective cohort, 1,401 major non-cardiac surgical patients; 28 death/MI events at 30 d. | Subjective capacity identified <4 MET on CPET with only 19.2% sensitivity. Only DASI was associated with the primary death/MI endpoint; do not attribute that result to NT-proBNP as well. | Structured DASI is more useful than an unaided subjective estimate; biomarkers have separate prognostic evidence and guideline indications. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [RCRI (Lee)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10477528/) (Circulation 1999) | 4,315 patients: derivation 2,893, validation 1,422, elective major non-cardiac surgery. | Six predictors. Original 0/1/2/≥3-factor major-complication rates: derivation 0.5/1.3/4/9%; validation 0.4/0.9/7/11%. Do not mix with contemporary death/MI risk estimates. | The standard bedside risk index | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |

## 8.2 Acute MI, cardiogenic shock and supportive care (Topic 2)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10460813/) (NEJM 1999) | RCT, 302 patients with MI shock; early revascularisation vs initial medical stabilisation | 30-day mortality 46.7 vs 56.0% (not significant); 6-month mortality 50.3 vs 63.1% | Emergency revascularisation is the key treatment | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22920912/) (NEJM 2012) | RCT, 600 patients; IABP vs none | 30-day mortality 39.7 vs 41.3% | No routine IABP in MI shock | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [CULPRIT-SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083953/) (NEJM 2017) | 706 randomised with MI shock and multivessel CAD; 685 in primary endpoint analysis. Culprit-only (staged PCI allowed) vs immediate multivessel PCI. | Death or renal replacement at 30 days lower with culprit-only (45.9 vs 55.4%) | Initial culprit-only strategy preferred in shock; staged treatment can follow. This is not a prohibition on ever treating other significant vessels. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [DanGer Shock](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38587239/) (NEJM 2024) | 360 randomised, 355 analysed (179 pump/176 control); selected STEMI-related shock, Impella CP plus standard care vs standard care. | 180 d death 45.8% vs 58.5% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55–0.99); safety composite 24.0% vs 6.2%; RRT 41.9% vs 26.7%. | Benefit in a selected STEMI-shock population with more complications; not generalisable to all shock, isolated RV failure or persistent coma after out-of-hospital arrest. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [ECLS-SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37634145/) (NEJM 2023) | 420 randomised, 417 analysed; early ECLS/VA-ECMO vs usual care in infarct-related shock. | 30 d death 47.8% vs 49.0% (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.80–1.19); moderate/severe bleeding 23.4% vs 9.6%; vascular intervention 11.0% vs 3.8%. | VA-ECMO does not routinely improve survival in MI shock | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [SOAP II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20200382/) (NEJM 2010) | RCT, 1,679 patients with shock; dopamine vs noradrenaline | 28 d death 52.5% dopamine vs 48.5% noradrenaline (P=.10); arrhythmia 24.1% vs 12.4%. Cardiogenic subgroup mortality signal favoured noradrenaline, with subgroup limitations. | Noradrenaline first line | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [DETO2X-AMI](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28844200/) (NEJM 2017) | 6,629 suspected MI patients, baseline SpO2 ≥90%; oxygen 6 L/min vs ambient air. | 1 y death 5.0% vs 5.1% (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.79–1.21); no significant benefit or definitive harm demonstrated. | No oxygen if SpO2 is 90% or more | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [MINT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37952133/) (NEJM 2023) | 3,504 patients with MI and Hb <100 g/L; restrictive 70/80 g/L vs liberal <100 g/L transfusion strategy. | 30 d death/MI 16.9% vs 14.5% (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.99–1.34; P=.07). Liberal superiority not established; clinically important harm from restriction could not be excluded. | Do not be aggressive about restrictive thresholds in acute MI | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |

## 8.3 Heart failure and pulmonary oedema (Topics 3 and 5)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [PARADIGM-HF](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25176015/) (NEJM 2014) | 8,442 randomised symptomatic HF patients, LVEF initially ≤40% (later ≤35%); ARNI vs enalapril; median 27 mo. | CV death/first HF hospitalisation 21.8% vs 26.5% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73–0.87); run-in selected tolerators, trial stopped early for benefit. | ARNI is first-line in HFrEF | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [DAPA-HF](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31535829/) (NEJM 2019) | 4,744 patients, LVEF ≤40%, dapagliflozin vs placebo; median 18.2 mo. | Worsening HF/CV death 16.3% vs 21.2% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.85); benefit with and without diabetes. | SGLT2 inhibitors for HFrEF; hold before surgery | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [EMPEROR-Reduced](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32865377/) (NEJM 2020) | 3,730 patients, LVEF ≤40%, empagliflozin vs placebo; median 16 mo. | CV death/HF hospitalisation 19.4% vs 24.7% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65–0.86), driven mainly by HF events; do not infer individual mortality benefit from the composite. | Confirms SGLT2 inhibitor benefit | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [DOSE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21366472/) (NEJM 2011) | RCT, 308 patients with acute decompensated HF; bolus vs infusion and low vs high furosemide dose | No significant difference in either coprimary outcome (72 h global symptoms or mean creatinine change) for bolus vs infusion or high vs low dose. High dose improved secondary decongestion measures with more transient worsening renal function. | Titrate to congestion, urine output, renal function and electrolytes. Neutral primary comparisons do not establish identical efficacy or justify ignoring dose/mode. | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
| [ESCAPE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16204662/) (JAMA 2005) | 433 advanced HF patients; PAC-guided vs clinical-guided decongestion, not a trial of obligatory PAC in refractory shock. | Days alive out of hospital at 6 mo 133 vs 135 (P=.99); in-hospital adverse events 21.9% vs 11.5%. | No routine PAC in acute HF | Primary abstract/results checked; link in trial name. |
